name: Rulers and Dynasties
description: Fifty royal subjects — monarchs, emperors, dynasties, usurpers and pretenders across every era and region — each with twenty materially distinct episode slots, for calm long-form biography told one life at a time.
subjects: tyrants and kings of the Greek world
late Roman emperors of the West
Capetian and Valois kings of France
Habsburg rulers of Spain and Austria
Korean kings of Goryeo and Joseon
the early caliphs and the Umayyads
kings of Ghana, Mali and Songhai
kings of Kongo, Benin and the Zulu
Mongol khans and the successor khanates

the Persian and Rus chronicles and the destruction layers in the trading cities
his court histories, the puppet khans' coinage, and the surviving monuments
the brief notices in several histories and the eastern diplomatic context
a contemporary soldier's history and the coin issues of the usurpation
the narrative histories and the brief coin series
the chronicles and the surviving encyclical texts
the chronicles and the coin portraits of the new regime
the chronicles and the terms of the settlement they record
the chronicle account and the later hagiographies of his brothers
a saga written at his direction and the church's hostile correspondence
the Byzantine histories and the Bulgarian chronicle notices
the chronicles of the reception and the trial records
the surviving correspondence, the parliamentary records, and the campaign accounts
the indentures of the disinherited and the campaign chronicles
the rebels' own written manifesto and the trial records

exclusions: No invented quotations, invented private thoughts, invented letters, or invented scenes; describe only what the record supports and say plainly where it stops.
No living people and nobody within living memory: every subject is a ruler long dead, and no descendant, claimant, or present-day political figure is named.
No hooks, cliffhangers, countdowns, teasers, or alarm of any kind, at the opening of a chapter or anywhere inside it.
No dwelling on torture, execution, battlefield injury, or sexual violence; state briefly that it happened and give the aftermath the time instead.
Keep every chapter self-contained and resolving to a quiet close, with no reference forward to a later chapter and no callback to an earlier one.
No verdict passed on a subject as hero or monster, no moralising, and no direct address urging the listener to do anything.
No modern political analogy, no claim about a present-day state, people, religion, or party, and no partisan framing of a contested national history.
prompt_context: Each chapter is the life of one ruler, told slowly for a listener already drifting toward sleep. Anchor the chapter to one court, one realm, and one definite stretch of years, and stay inside them rather than sweeping across a dynasty. Explain how the office actually worked — how an heir was chosen, how a treasury was filled, who was allowed into a room, what a coronation required, what a governor was expected to send and when — and let the explanation itself be the interest. Favour material and administrative detail over incident: the weight of a crown, the wording of an oath, the price of a campaign, the size of a household, the road a court travelled and the estates it ate its way through. Do not open with a hook, a question, or a promise; begin inside the reign. Do not build tension, withhold information, or end a chapter pointing forward. Where a battle, a murder, a deposition, or an execution belongs to the life, describe it plainly and briefly and give the aftermath more time than the act. Name the subject and other historical figures as the record names them, invent nobody, and quote nothing that was not written down. Keep sentences unhurried and mostly declarative, and let paragraphs settle rather than accelerate. End each chapter on a still image — a sealed charter, an empty audience hall, a tomb effigy, a coin worn smooth — so that a listener who drifts off loses nothing.

idea_axes.label: Royal-biography lens
values: the household, the court, and access to the ruler
war, the army, and the frontier
religion, ritual, and the sacred office
monument, memory, and the shaping of a reputation

tuples.episode_object: Narmer, the first king shown wearing both crowns at once
tuples.time_place_scope: the Nile valley and the delta at the opening of the dynastic age
tuples.mechanism: unification by conquest and ceremony together, where a single wearer of two crowns made one office out of two countries
tuples.evidence_lens: carved ceremonial palettes and mace heads read against the earliest royal cemeteries

tuples.episode_object: Hor-Aha, the early king remembered for founding a capital where two lands met
tuples.time_place_scope: the head of the delta through the First Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the placing of a royal residence at a hinge point, so that administration rather than an army held the country together
tuples.evidence_lens: tomb enclosures and sealings compared with later king lists

tuples.episode_object: Den, the king whose reign left the first careful year-by-year record
tuples.time_place_scope: Egypt and the eastern desert margins through the First Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the naming of years by their events, which turned a reign into a countable, auditable thing
tuples.evidence_lens: year labels and annal fragments set beside subsidiary burials

tuples.episode_object: Djoser, the king who put six stone steps where a mud rectangle had stood
tuples.time_place_scope: the desert plateau above the old capital in the Third Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the shift from brick to dressed stone, which required a permanent quarrying and labour organisation and thereby created one
tuples.evidence_lens: quarry marks and construction phases read against the earliest architect's titles

tuples.episode_object: Sekhemkhet, the king whose pyramid was abandoned at the second course
tuples.time_place_scope: the same plateau across a short reign in the Third Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the dependence of a monument on the life of its owner, since work stopped the day the funding did
tuples.evidence_lens: unfinished enclosures and their sealed foundation deposits

tuples.episode_object: Huni, the last king of his line and the first to leave small pyramids far from home
tuples.time_place_scope: the length of the Nile valley at the close of the Third Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: provincial monuments as markers of royal presence in places the court itself rarely reached
tuples.evidence_lens: the distribution of small step pyramids compared with regional administrative titles

tuples.episode_object: Sneferu, the king who built three pyramids while learning how to build one
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern desert edge across a long Fourth Dynasty reign
tuples.mechanism: iterative engineering, in which a collapsed angle and a changed slope are corrections rather than failures
tuples.evidence_lens: internal cracking, casing angles, and dated builders' graffiti

tuples.episode_object: Khufu, the king better attested by his workforce than by himself
tuples.time_place_scope: the great plateau and the river quarries through the Fourth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the logistics of a state building project — bread, beer, rotation, and boats — rather than the mystery of the stones
tuples.evidence_lens: workmen's settlements, bakery installations, and a harbour journal of stone deliveries

tuples.episode_object: Djedefre, the king who moved the family cemetery and was later scratched out of it
tuples.time_place_scope: a high desert site north of the plateau in the Fourth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the deliberate erasure of a predecessor, which tells more about the successor than about the erased
tuples.evidence_lens: defaced statuary and a partly quarried pyramid site

tuples.episode_object: Khafre, the king whose face may sit on a lion's body at the edge of his causeway
tuples.time_place_scope: the plateau and its quarries through the Fourth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the reuse of a quarry scar as sculpture, so that the waste of one project became the guardian of the next
tuples.evidence_lens: geological bedding in the carved body compared with adjacent quarry faces

tuples.episode_object: Menkaure, the king with the smallest of the three great pyramids and the finest statuary
tuples.time_place_scope: the plateau in the later Fourth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the substitution of craftsmanship for scale, as a smaller monument absorbed the same skilled labour in finish
tuples.evidence_lens: unfinished granite casing and paired greywacke statue groups

tuples.episode_object: Shepseskaf, the king who chose a great stone bench instead of a pyramid
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern desert cemeteries at the end of the Fourth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: a deliberate break in royal funerary form, which signalled a change of priesthood and patronage
tuples.evidence_lens: the mastaba tomb form set against contemporary temple endowments

tuples.episode_object: Userkaf, the king who built a temple to the sun beside his own tomb
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern cemeteries at the opening of the Fifth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the rise of a solar cult with its own estates, which put a second institution beside the king's own
tuples.evidence_lens: sun temple foundations and their attached estate lists

tuples.episode_object: Sahure, the king whose causeway reliefs record fleets returning from a distant coast
tuples.time_place_scope: the Nile valley and the Red Sea approaches in the Fifth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: royal expeditions as economic policy, bringing back resin, timber, and metal that no local estate could supply
tuples.evidence_lens: causeway relief programmes read against expedition inscriptions in the eastern desert

tuples.episode_object: Nyuserre, the king who inherited a family's unfinished monuments and completed them
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern cemeteries through a long Fifth Dynasty reign
tuples.mechanism: the completion of a predecessor's works as a claim of continuity, cheaper than starting again
tuples.evidence_lens: building phases and reused blocks in adjoining complexes

tuples.episode_object: Djedkare Isesi, the king who broke with the sun temples and promoted officials from outside the family
tuples.time_place_scope: the court and the provinces in the later Fifth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the widening of high office beyond royal kin, which bought competence at the price of a rival elite
tuples.evidence_lens: changing title strings in officials' tombs and their tomb sizes

tuples.episode_object: Unas, the king who first had the spells for the afterlife carved on his burial chamber walls
tuples.time_place_scope: the old capital's cemetery at the close of the Fifth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the writing down of ritual, which fixed a liturgy that had been spoken and made it copyable
tuples.evidence_lens: the earliest pyramid texts compared with later recensions

tuples.episode_object: Teti, the king whose bodyguards are said to have killed him
tuples.time_place_scope: the court at the opening of the Sixth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the vulnerability of a palace regime to its own household troops, and how a succession absorbs a violent death
tuples.evidence_lens: a single later report of the killing weighed against contemporary silence in the tombs

tuples.episode_object: Pepi I, the king who tried a conspiracy in the harem in secret and had it written down anyway
tuples.time_place_scope: the royal residence and the southern provinces in the Sixth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the private royal enquiry, an instrument that kept a scandal out of the courts and inside the household
tuples.evidence_lens: an official's autobiographical tomb inscription describing the hearing

tuples.episode_object: Pepi II, the king credited with the longest reign and the thinning of the state that followed it
tuples.time_place_scope: Egypt and the Nubian trade routes across most of the Sixth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the slow devolution of revenue to provincial governors, which hollowed a court that outlived its own settlement
tuples.evidence_lens: provincial tomb wealth measured against declining royal endowments

tuples.episode_object: Ahmose, the king who finished a war of expulsion begun by his father and brother
tuples.time_place_scope: the delta and the eastern frontier at the opening of the Eighteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the conversion of a dynastic war of liberation into a standing frontier army
tuples.evidence_lens: a marine's autobiographical tomb text read against siege archaeology in the delta

tuples.episode_object: Hatshepsut, the queen who took the full titulary and was later chiselled off the walls
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern capital and a Red Sea trading route in the Eighteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: female kingship expressed through borrowed male regalia, and the later erasure that admits it worked
tuples.evidence_lens: expedition reliefs and systematically defaced cartouches

tuples.episode_object: Thutmose III, the co-ruler who waited twenty years and then campaigned for twenty more
tuples.time_place_scope: the Levantine corridor across successive campaign seasons in the Eighteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: annual campaigning as a revenue system, where tribute schedules mattered more than battles
tuples.evidence_lens: temple annals listing spoils and tribute, checked against Levantine destruction layers

tuples.episode_object: Amenhotep III, the king whose reign is measured in statues rather than campaigns
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern capital and its west bank through a long peaceful reign
tuples.mechanism: diplomatic marriage and gift exchange as an alternative to war, funded by gold the neighbours wanted
tuples.evidence_lens: diplomatic letter archives and mass-produced royal statuary

tuples.episode_object: Akhenaten, the king who moved a capital to empty ground for a single god
tuples.time_place_scope: a virgin desert bay in Middle Egypt across a short reign
tuples.mechanism: a state religious reform imposed from the throne, and the administrative cost of relocating a court
tuples.evidence_lens: boundary stelae, a purpose-built city plan, and abandoned diplomatic correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Tutankhamun, the boy king restored to orthodoxy by the men who ran his government
tuples.time_place_scope: the old capitals during the reversal of the reform
tuples.mechanism: regency in all but name, where a restoration decree carries a child's name and an official's policy
tuples.evidence_lens: a restoration stela read against the careers of the officials who followed him

tuples.episode_object: Horemheb, the general who became king and wrote himself into the reigns before him
tuples.time_place_scope: the court and the army camps at the end of the Eighteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: legitimation by legal reform, buying consent with an edict against official extortion
tuples.evidence_lens: a great edict text set beside the recutting of earlier monuments

tuples.episode_object: Seti I, the king whose temple reliefs are the finest and whose frontier was the busiest
tuples.time_place_scope: the Levant and the desert wells through the early Nineteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the fortified well road, which made an army's march a matter of water rather than distance
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign reliefs compared with excavated frontier forts and wells

tuples.episode_object: Ramesses II, the king who lost the initiative at a river crossing and won the wall space
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern Levant and the delta residence across a very long reign
tuples.mechanism: monumental publicity, in which the account of an event outlives the event and shapes the record
tuples.evidence_lens: parallel accounts of one battle in two states' archives and a surviving treaty text

tuples.episode_object: Merneptah, the elderly heir who spent his reign fighting people arriving by sea and desert
tuples.time_place_scope: the western delta and the Libyan margin in the late Nineteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: defensive settlement of defeated migrants inside the frontier, a policy of absorption rather than expulsion
tuples.evidence_lens: a victory stela listing peoples, read against western fort garrison lists

tuples.episode_object: Tausret, the queen who ruled alone at the end of a collapsing dynasty
tuples.time_place_scope: the court through a disputed succession in the Nineteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: regency hardening into sole rule when no adult male claimant survives the family
tuples.evidence_lens: a usurped tomb and altered cartouches in a royal valley

tuples.episode_object: Ramesses III, the king who fought off invasion and then could not pay his own workmen
tuples.time_place_scope: the delta coast and the royal workmen's village in the Twentieth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the ration economy of a state without coinage, where a late grain delivery is a political crisis
tuples.evidence_lens: a workmen's village journal recording the first recorded strike, and temple endowment lists

tuples.episode_object: Ramesses IX, the king whose reign is documented by the trials of the men robbing royal tombs
tuples.time_place_scope: the western cemeteries of the southern capital in the Twentieth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: tomb robbery as an index of state weakness, when the guard becomes the thief
tuples.evidence_lens: court papyri recording confessions, inspections, and the reburial of kings

tuples.episode_object: Ramesses XI, the last king of a line who ruled a country already run by two other men
tuples.time_place_scope: the divided north and south at the close of the New Kingdom
tuples.mechanism: the quiet partition of authority between a northern soldier and a southern high priest
tuples.evidence_lens: a renaming of the era in dated documents and the correspondence of a travelling envoy

tuples.episode_object: Amenhotep II, the athlete king who advertised his own bowmanship as a qualification
tuples.time_place_scope: the Levantine corridor and the southern capital in the Eighteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: physical prowess as a public argument for fitness to rule in a warrior monarchy
tuples.evidence_lens: sporting stelae and a chariot training text compared with campaign records

tuples.episode_object: Thutmose IV, the prince who said a sphinx told him in a dream he would be king
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern plateau in the Eighteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the dream oracle as a legitimation device for a son who was not the obvious heir
tuples.evidence_lens: a stela set between a sphinx's paws, read against the birth order of the royal sons

tuples.episode_object: Smenkhkare, the shadowy co-ruler nobody can securely identify
tuples.time_place_scope: the reform capital in its final years
tuples.mechanism: the limits of the record, where titles survive but the body behind them does not
tuples.evidence_lens: contested cartouches, a disputed mummy, and shifting scholarly identifications

tuples.episode_object: Ay, the elderly courtier who took the throne after serving three kings
tuples.time_place_scope: the court in the closing years of the Eighteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the succession of a household official when a royal line runs out of bodies
tuples.evidence_lens: tomb decoration showing the burial rite performed by the successor

tuples.episode_object: Siptah, the boy king with a withered foot and a powerful chancellor
tuples.time_place_scope: the court through a contested reign in the Nineteenth Dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the chancellor as the real executive during a minority, and the erasure that follows his fall
tuples.evidence_lens: a royal mummy's pathology set beside the defaced monuments of the chancellor

tuples.episode_object: Setnakhte, the founder who claimed he ended a period of anarchy nobody else describes
tuples.time_place_scope: the delta and the valley between two dynasties
tuples.mechanism: the restoration narrative, in which a new house justifies itself by the disorder it says it ended
tuples.evidence_lens: a single long stela weighed against the absence of corroborating documents

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the son of Lagos, the general who took a dead king's body and made it a claim
tuples.time_place_scope: Egypt and the Levantine coast in the decades after the conquest
tuples.mechanism: the possession of a founder's corpse as a legitimating relic in a contested succession
tuples.evidence_lens: contemporary campaign histories preserved in later summaries, and early coin portraits

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Second, the king who married his sister and funded a library
tuples.time_place_scope: the new coastal capital across a long third-century reign
tuples.mechanism: the endowment of scholarship as royal display, and sibling marriage as a way to keep a claim inside one household
tuples.evidence_lens: foundation records, temple decrees, and the surviving book lists of a great collection

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Third, the king who marched east and came home to a revolt in the countryside
tuples.time_place_scope: the Levant, Mesopotamia, and the Egyptian interior in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the strain of a distant campaign on an agricultural tax base that had to be collected in person
tuples.evidence_lens: a trilingual priestly decree and tax registers from village archives

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Fourth, the king who won a battle by arming Egyptians and could not disarm them
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern frontier and the Nile valley at the end of the third century
tuples.mechanism: the political consequence of recruiting a subject population into a phalanx
tuples.evidence_lens: battle accounts read against a long secession in the south recorded in dated contracts

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Fifth, the child on whose behalf the priests wrote a stone in three scripts
tuples.time_place_scope: the old capital and the delta in the early second century
tuples.mechanism: the negotiated decree, in which a weak throne buys priestly support with tax remissions
tuples.evidence_lens: a trilingual decree whose bargain is stated in its own text

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Sixth, the king who ruled alongside a brother who kept trying to remove him
tuples.time_place_scope: Egypt and a rising western power's diplomatic orbit in the second century
tuples.mechanism: joint rule as an arbitration outcome imposed by an outside power
tuples.evidence_lens: embassy accounts and a partition settlement recorded in inscriptions

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Eighth, the king whose nickname mocked his body and whose reign emptied a capital
tuples.time_place_scope: the coastal capital and the Nile valley in the later second century
tuples.mechanism: the political expulsion of a professional class, and the export of scholarship it caused
tuples.evidence_lens: an amnesty decree and scattered evidence of scholars relocating

tuples.episode_object: Cleopatra the Third, the queen who used her sons against each other for thirty years
tuples.time_place_scope: the court and the southern temples in the later second century
tuples.mechanism: maternal regency sustained by controlling which son held which province
tuples.evidence_lens: co-regency dating formulas in dated legal documents

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Twelfth, the king who borrowed foreign money to buy recognition of his own throne
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and a foreign creditor's political marketplace in the first century
tuples.mechanism: debt diplomacy, in which recognition is purchased and the interest is collected from a country
tuples.evidence_lens: loan arrangements described in political speeches and later histories

tuples.episode_object: Berenice the Fourth, the daughter who ruled while her father was abroad raising the loan
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital across a short interregnum in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the caretaker reign that becomes a rival claim the moment the absent ruler returns
tuples.evidence_lens: dated documents in her name and the record of her removal

tuples.episode_object: Cleopatra the Seventh, the last ruler of the house and the only one said to have learned the language
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital, the Levant, and a foreign civil war in the first century
tuples.mechanism: personal diplomacy with a foreign commander as the only remaining instrument of a small state
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile foreign histories set against Egyptian temple reliefs and coin portraits

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Thirteenth, the boy king whose advisers killed a guest to please a stronger one
tuples.time_place_scope: the delta coast during a foreign civil war
tuples.mechanism: the courtier council governing for a minor, and its catastrophic misreading of an outside power
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign memoirs of the foreign commander read against Egyptian dating formulas

tuples.episode_object: Arsinoe the Fourth, the sister who was proclaimed by an army and then paraded as a captive
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and a foreign city in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the making of a rival monarch by acclamation in a besieged city
tuples.evidence_lens: a triumph description and a disputed tomb identification

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Ninth, the son twice removed from the throne by his own mother
tuples.time_place_scope: Egypt and a Mediterranean island exile in the later second century
tuples.mechanism: exile as a holding position, kept viable by a province that still recognised the exile
tuples.evidence_lens: island dating formulas and later restoration documents

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Tenth, the brother who reigned by his mother's preference and died at sea
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the eastern Mediterranean in the early first century
tuples.mechanism: the pledging of a kingdom as security for a loan, and the claim it later created
tuples.evidence_lens: references to a testamentary bequest in foreign political debate

tuples.episode_object: Arsinoe the Second, the queen given a cult of her own while a temple economy grew around it
tuples.time_place_scope: the delta and the coastal capital in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the ruler cult as fiscal architecture, with priesthoods, estates, and a tax attached
tuples.evidence_lens: cult decrees and temple estate accounts

tuples.episode_object: Cleopatra the Second, the queen who fought a civil war against her own brother-husband
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the southern provinces in the later second century
tuples.mechanism: the co-regency turning into two rival governments issuing documents in parallel
tuples.evidence_lens: competing dating formulas in contracts from the same years

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy the Eleventh, the king who reigned for nineteen days and was killed by a crowd
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the early first century
tuples.mechanism: the urban crowd as an actor in dynastic politics in a capital city
tuples.evidence_lens: brief notices in later chronicles and a gap in dated documents

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy Apion, the ruler of a western province who willed it to a foreign republic
tuples.time_place_scope: the Libyan coast in the late second century
tuples.mechanism: testamentary bequest of a kingdom, a legal device that transferred a state without a war
tuples.evidence_lens: the bequest recorded in foreign senatorial debate and provincial reorganisation

tuples.episode_object: Caesarion, the boy proclaimed co-ruler and killed to end a claim
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the southern desert road in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the elimination of a claimant as an administrative act at the close of a dynasty
tuples.evidence_lens: temple reliefs naming him beside later hostile accounts of his death

tuples.episode_object: Sargon, the cupbearer who took a throne and called himself king of the whole land
tuples.time_place_scope: the Mesopotamian floodplain and the trade roads beyond it
tuples.mechanism: the first attempt at a territorial empire, held by garrisons and a standard measure rather than by tribute alone
tuples.evidence_lens: later copied royal inscriptions and the distribution of a standardised script

tuples.episode_object: Rimush, the son who spent his reign putting down the cities his father had taken
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern cities in the Akkadian period
tuples.mechanism: the succession revolt, in which conquered cities test a new king rather than an old one
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign inscriptions listing city by city, read against destruction layers

tuples.episode_object: Naram-Sin, the king who wrote a divine determinative in front of his own name
tuples.time_place_scope: the floodplain and the northern hill country
tuples.mechanism: royal deification, an explicit claim that shifted a king from servant of the gods to one of them
tuples.evidence_lens: a victory stela and the writing conventions of his own inscriptions

tuples.episode_object: Shar-kali-sharri, the last strong king of a house whose empire dissolved after him
tuples.time_place_scope: the floodplain during a period of drought and incursion
tuples.mechanism: the failure of a supply system when climate and raiding hit the same decades
tuples.evidence_lens: year names, ration texts, and palaeoclimate sequences

tuples.episode_object: Ur-Nammu, the king who wrote a law collection before anybody else we can read
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern cities at the founding of a new dynasty
tuples.mechanism: the published law code as a claim of justice rather than a working statute book
tuples.evidence_lens: a prologue and tariff of penalties on copied tablets

tuples.episode_object: Shulgi, the king who reorganised a state around measurement, months, and messengers
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern cities and their provincial capitals
tuples.mechanism: the bureaucratic state, in which standard weights, a calendar, and a courier system make taxation legible
tuples.evidence_lens: tens of thousands of administrative tablets from provincial archives

tuples.episode_object: Ibbi-Sin, the king who watched provinces stop sending grain one by one
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern cities in a failing final decade
tuples.mechanism: the fiscal secession of provinces, visible as prices rise and deliveries cease
tuples.evidence_lens: grain price records and the correspondence of a provincial officer

tuples.episode_object: Hammurabi, the king whose stone of laws outlived the kingdom it was written for
tuples.time_place_scope: the middle floodplain across a long reign
tuples.mechanism: codification as a public standard against which a king could be measured, and the diplomacy that preceded the conquests
tuples.evidence_lens: the law stela itself and a large royal letter archive from an allied palace

tuples.episode_object: Samsu-iluna, the heir who lost the south to salt, rebellion, and a rival house
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern marshes and canals in the following generation

tuples.evidence_lens: his own coinage and the accounts of two neighbouring historiographies

tuples.episode_object: Khosrow the Second, the king who reached a foreign capital's suburbs and lost everything after
tuples.time_place_scope: the Levant, Egypt, Anatolia, and the plateau in the early seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the maximal conquest that outruns the logistics and the political settlement needed to keep it
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign chronicles, occupation papyri from Egypt, and coin distributions

tuples.episode_object: Shirin, the queen whose Christianity sat inside a Zoroastrian court
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and its churches in the early seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the confessional queen as a channel between a state religion and a large minority
tuples.evidence_lens: church histories and later romance traditions read apart

tuples.episode_object: Borandokht, the daughter who took the throne in a year of many claimants
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital during the post-war collapse
tuples.mechanism: female accession as a last resort when the male line has consumed itself
tuples.evidence_lens: coins struck in her name and a compressed chronicle sequence

tuples.episode_object: Yazdegerd the Third, the last shahanshah, crowned as a child into a losing war
tuples.time_place_scope: the plateau and the eastern provinces in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the fugitive court, whose authority survives only as long as a provincial governor honours it
tuples.evidence_lens: conquest-era chronicles, coin mints, and a datable regnal era

tuples.episode_object: Ardashir the Third, the boy king killed by a general within two years
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the child placed on a throne by a faction that cannot defend him
tuples.evidence_lens: a very short coin series and chronicle notices

tuples.episode_object: Shapur the Third, the king who signed away half of a client kingdom to end a war
tuples.time_place_scope: the Armenian highlands in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the partition of a buffer kingdom as a durable settlement between two empires
tuples.evidence_lens: Armenian and Byzantine accounts of the partition

tuples.episode_object: Kavad the Second, the son who killed his brothers and reigned for months
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital during the plague years of the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the fratricidal accession that removes every alternative and leaves none
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle accounts and epidemic notices in the same years

tuples.episode_object: Azarmidokht, the second queen of the collapse, deposed by a frontier commander
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the provincial army commander as the effective elector in a failing state
tuples.evidence_lens: a brief coin issue and conflicting chronicle notices

tuples.episode_object: Philip the Second, the hostage prince who came home and rebuilt an army from the ranks up
tuples.time_place_scope: the Macedonian plain and the Greek city-states in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the reformed infantry line, paid and drilled year-round, which made a marginal kingdom central
tuples.evidence_lens: contemporary political speeches, later histories, and battlefield archaeology

tuples.episode_object: Alexander the Third, the king who never lost a battle and never arranged a succession
tuples.time_place_scope: Anatolia, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Indus in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the failure to designate an heir, which converted a personal empire into a forty-year war
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign histories from participants' lost memoirs, and administrative continuity in conquered provinces

tuples.episode_object: Philip the Third, the half-brother with an impairment who was carried around as a legitimacy token
tuples.time_place_scope: the whole contested empire after the conquest
tuples.mechanism: the puppet king whose body legitimises whoever holds it
tuples.evidence_lens: regnal dating formulas in Babylonian tablets and later narrative histories

tuples.episode_object: Alexander the Fourth, the posthumous son kept alive until he became dangerous
tuples.time_place_scope: Macedonia and the Aegean in the late fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the minority that ends the moment the child approaches an age to rule
tuples.evidence_lens: a royal tomb complex and the chronology of dated documents

tuples.episode_object: Olympias, the mother who took a regency and executed her way through a faction
tuples.time_place_scope: Macedonia and the western Greek states
tuples.mechanism: the dynastic matriarch as a faction leader in her own right, with her own troops and clients
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile later histories and inscriptional honours from Greek states

tuples.episode_object: Antipater, the regent who governed the homeland while the army marched east
tuples.time_place_scope: Macedonia and the Greek mainland in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the home regency, whose control of recruitment outweighs distant victories
tuples.evidence_lens: letters reported in later histories and Athenian decrees

tuples.episode_object: Perdiccas, the officer who held the royal seal and lost the army to a river crossing
tuples.time_place_scope: Egypt and the Nile delta in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the custodianship of royal authority, which is only as strong as the soldiers' willingness to obey it
tuples.evidence_lens: the successor histories and the Egyptian route archaeology

tuples.episode_object: Antigonus the One-Eyed, the old general who nearly reassembled the whole empire
tuples.time_place_scope: Anatolia, the Levant, and the Aegean in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the coalition that forms automatically against whichever successor grows strongest
tuples.evidence_lens: city decrees granting honours, and campaign narratives

tuples.episode_object: Demetrius the Besieger, the king famous for a siege he did not win
tuples.time_place_scope: the Aegean islands and mainland Greece
tuples.mechanism: siege engineering as spectacle, and the political capital of a magnificent failure
tuples.evidence_lens: technical siege descriptions and civic monuments

tuples.episode_object: Seleucus the First, the officer who founded more cities than anyone and died crossing a strait
tuples.time_place_scope: Mesopotamia, Iran, and the Anatolian coast
tuples.mechanism: city foundation as an occupation strategy, settling veterans where roads and rivers meet
tuples.evidence_lens: foundation inscriptions, city plans, and cuneiform chronicles

tuples.episode_object: Lysimachus, the king of a northern kingdom who lost it at eighty
tuples.time_place_scope: Thrace and western Anatolia in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the personal kingdom that cannot survive its founder because it has no institutions
tuples.evidence_lens: coin issues, city refoundations, and a battle narrative

tuples.episode_object: Cassander, the son who executed a royal family and founded a city named for a queen
tuples.time_place_scope: Macedonia and the Greek cities in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the elimination of the old royal line as a precondition for a new one
tuples.evidence_lens: city foundation evidence and hostile historiography

tuples.episode_object: Pyrrhus, the king who won battles at costs he could not repeat
tuples.time_place_scope: western Greece, Italy, and Sicily in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the expeditionary monarchy funded by campaign, which fails when a war stops paying
tuples.evidence_lens: his own lost memoirs quoted by later writers, and Italian battle sites

tuples.episode_object: Antigonus Gonatas, the king who stabilised a kingdom by garrisoning three fortresses
tuples.time_place_scope: Macedonia and the Greek mainland in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the strategic garrison, holding a country with a handful of strongpoints instead of an army in the field
tuples.evidence_lens: garrison inscriptions and civic decrees complaining about them

tuples.episode_object: Antiochus the Third, the king who marched to the east and then lost the west
tuples.time_place_scope: Iran, India's approaches, and the Aegean in the third and second centuries
tuples.mechanism: the anabasis that restores prestige without restoring control, and the indemnity that follows defeat
tuples.evidence_lens: treaty terms recorded by foreign historians and eastern coin evidence

tuples.episode_object: Antiochus the Fourth, the king whose interference in a temple state started a long revolt
tuples.time_place_scope: the Levant and the eastern Mediterranean in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the fiscal raid on temple treasuries, which converts a money problem into a religious war
tuples.evidence_lens: two partisan Jewish histories and Greek chronicle notices

tuples.episode_object: Philip the Fifth, the king who fought a western republic twice and lost both times
tuples.time_place_scope: Macedonia, the Aegean, and Greece in the third and second centuries
tuples.mechanism: the small kingdom caught between a rising western power and its Greek clients
tuples.evidence_lens: treaty inscriptions and a foreign historian's account written from senate records

tuples.episode_object: Perseus, the last king of Macedonia, paraded through a foreign city in a triumph
tuples.time_place_scope: Macedonia and Italy in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the dismemberment of a kingdom into republics, a settlement designed to prevent its revival
tuples.evidence_lens: the settlement terms in foreign histories and Macedonian coinage ending

tuples.episode_object: Eumenes of Cardia, the secretary who out-generalled generals and was betrayed by his own troops
tuples.time_place_scope: Anatolia and Iran in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the outsider commander, obeyed for competence and abandoned for lack of birth
tuples.evidence_lens: a detailed successor narrative and the record of veteran units changing sides

tuples.episode_object: Ptolemy Keraunos, the claimant who took a throne and lost his head to an invasion
tuples.time_place_scope: Macedonia and the northern frontier in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the frontier invasion that arrives while a succession is still unsettled
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle notices and the record of a Greek sanctuary's defence

coverage_profiles.subject: tyrants and kings of the Greek world

tuples.episode_object: Peisistratus, the tyrant who took a city three times and governed it lightly
tuples.time_place_scope: an Attic city and its countryside in the sixth century
tuples.mechanism: the popular tyranny, which funds rural smallholders and festivals against an aristocracy
tuples.evidence_lens: later constitutional histories and archaeological evidence of building programmes

tuples.episode_object: Polycrates, the island tyrant who built a tunnel and financed a fleet by raiding
tuples.time_place_scope: an eastern Aegean island in the sixth century
tuples.mechanism: the maritime tyranny funded by piracy and public works, and its dependence on one man's luck
tuples.evidence_lens: a surviving rock-cut aqueduct and narrative histories

tuples.episode_object: Cypselus, the exile who returned to take a wealthy trading city
tuples.time_place_scope: an isthmus city in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the tyrant emerging from an excluded aristocratic branch rather than from the poor
tuples.evidence_lens: dedications at panhellenic sanctuaries and later histories

tuples.episode_object: Periander, the tyrant remembered as both a sage and a monster
tuples.time_place_scope: the isthmus city and its two harbours
tuples.mechanism: the contradictory tradition, in which a ruler is listed among the wise and accused of atrocities
tuples.evidence_lens: wisdom traditions set against hostile anecdote collections

tuples.episode_object: Cleisthenes of Sicyon, the tyrant who renamed the tribes to insult his neighbours
tuples.time_place_scope: a northern Peloponnesian city in the sixth century
tuples.mechanism: tribal reorganisation as a political instrument, redrawing who counts as a citizen bloc
tuples.evidence_lens: later histories preserving tribe names and civic cult changes

tuples.episode_object: Gelon, the Sicilian ruler who moved whole populations to fill a capital
tuples.time_place_scope: eastern Sicily in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: forced synoecism, in which a ruler dissolves cities to build one loyal population
tuples.evidence_lens: battle dedications, city archaeology, and later histories

tuples.episode_object: Hieron the First, the tyrant who hired the best poets in Greece to describe him
tuples.time_place_scope: eastern Sicily in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: literary patronage as reputation management, commissioning odes that outlast the regime
tuples.evidence_lens: surviving victory odes and monumental dedications

tuples.episode_object: Dionysius the First, the ruler who invented a siege engine and a permanent war footing
tuples.time_place_scope: eastern Sicily and southern Italy in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the militarised state that keeps a citizenry mobilised by keeping a war open
tuples.evidence_lens: fortification archaeology, siege technology descriptions, and hostile histories

tuples.episode_object: Agathocles, the potter's son who took a city and invaded a rival's homeland
tuples.time_place_scope: Sicily and the North African coast in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the counter-invasion, taking the war to an enemy's home ground to break a siege at home
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign narratives and coin issues claiming a royal title

tuples.episode_object: Leonidas the First, the king remembered for a defeat he chose
tuples.time_place_scope: a narrow pass in central Greece in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the dual kingship and the ritual constraints that decided which king marched
tuples.evidence_lens: a foreign historian's narrative and the archaeology of the pass

tuples.episode_object: Cleomenes the First, the king who intervened everywhere and died strangely at home
tuples.time_place_scope: the Peloponnese and central Greece around the turn of the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the king who uses foreign policy to escape the constraints of a divided constitution
tuples.evidence_lens: narrative histories and the record of oracular manipulation

tuples.episode_object: Agesilaus the Second, the lame king who campaigned in Asia and lost the hegemony at home
tuples.time_place_scope: Anatolia and mainland Greece in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the hegemony that collapses when a professional enemy adopts the same tactics
tuples.evidence_lens: an admiring contemporary memoir and a critical later biography

tuples.episode_object: Agis the Fourth, the young king who tried to cancel debts and redistribute land
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern Peloponnese in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the reform monarchy attempting redistribution against a landowning elite, and the trial that ends it
tuples.evidence_lens: a later biography drawing on lost contemporary sources

tuples.episode_object: Cleomenes the Third, the king who completed the reform and lost the war
tuples.time_place_scope: the Peloponnese and Egypt in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the reformed army as the fiscal product of a land redistribution
tuples.evidence_lens: battlefield accounts and the record of an exile's death abroad

tuples.episode_object: Nabis, the last ruler of a reformed southern state, called a tyrant by everyone who wrote
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern Peloponnese in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the freeing of enslaved people as a recruitment measure, and the historiography it produced
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile narrative sources and inscriptions from occupied towns

tuples.episode_object: Jason of Pherae, the northern ruler who almost unified Thessaly before being murdered
tuples.time_place_scope: the Thessalian plain in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the federal office of an elected commander turned into a personal monarchy
tuples.evidence_lens: contemporary political pamphlets and later histories

tuples.episode_object: Mausolus, the satrap who ruled like a king and was buried like a god
tuples.time_place_scope: the south-western Anatolian coast in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the hellenised satrap, governing an empire's province in the idiom of a Greek dynast
tuples.evidence_lens: a monumental tomb's sculpture and civic inscriptions

tuples.episode_object: Archelaus of Macedon, the king who built roads and invited playwrights
tuples.time_place_scope: the Macedonian plain in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the infrastructure monarchy, buying integration with roads, forts, and a court culture
tuples.evidence_lens: a contemporary historian's brief notice and evidence of a court theatre

tuples.episode_object: Hiero the Second, the Sicilian king who kept one city neutral and rich for fifty years
tuples.time_place_scope: eastern Sicily during a long war between two great powers
tuples.mechanism: neutrality maintained by supplying both sides and by a tax law worth copying
tuples.evidence_lens: a grain tax law described by a later foreign source, and civic buildings

tuples.episode_object: Aratus of Sicyon, the federal statesman who ran a league like a monarch
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern Peloponnese in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the annual elected office held repeatedly, which turns a federal magistracy into a personal regime
tuples.evidence_lens: his own memoirs quoted by a later historian, and league decrees

tuples.episode_object: Augustus, the heir who kept every republican title and quietly kept the army too
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome, Italy, and the frontier provinces across a very long first reign
tuples.mechanism: the accumulation of ordinary magistracies into an extraordinary position, so that nothing was formally abolished
tuples.evidence_lens: his own funerary account of his deeds, coin legends, and building inscriptions

tuples.episode_object: Tiberius, the reluctant successor who governed an empire from an island
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and a southern island villa in the first century
tuples.mechanism: government by correspondence, and what happens to a senate when the ruler stops attending
tuples.evidence_lens: a senatorial history written a century later, weighed against surviving senate decrees

tuples.episode_object: Caligula, the young emperor whose reign is known almost entirely from hostile pens
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome, the northern frontier, and the Channel coast
tuples.mechanism: the assassination narrative, which requires the victim to have been mad for the killers to be right
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile biographies read against inscriptions, coins, and building accounts

tuples.episode_object: Claudius, the scholar found behind a curtain and made emperor by the guard
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome, the harbour works, and the British campaign
tuples.mechanism: the guard's donative, which made an army unit the effective elector of an emperor
tuples.evidence_lens: coin issues advertising the accession, and a surviving speech on provincial citizenship

tuples.episode_object: Nero, the emperor who lost the provinces before he lost the city
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome, Greece, and the Gallic and Spanish provinces
tuples.mechanism: the provincial governor's revolt, which showed that legitimacy sat with the legions
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile histories, coin hoards, and inscriptions from the year of the revolts

tuples.episode_object: Livia, the empress who outlived her husband by fifteen years and shaped two reigns
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the imperial estates across three reigns
tuples.mechanism: the imperial widow's patronage network, exercised through clients rather than through office
tuples.evidence_lens: her surviving villa and a senate decree recording honours refused and granted

tuples.episode_object: Marcus Agrippa, the deputy who won the wars and never took the first place
tuples.time_place_scope: the Mediterranean, Gaul, and the eastern provinces
tuples.mechanism: the co-ruler in fact without the title, given the powers but not the primacy
tuples.evidence_lens: his building programme in the capital and the grants of tribunician power

tuples.episode_object: Germanicus, the heir apparent who died in the east amid accusations of poison
tuples.time_place_scope: the Rhine frontier, Egypt, and Syria
tuples.mechanism: the popular heir whose death becomes a political crisis and then a trial
tuples.evidence_lens: a surviving senatorial decree recording the trial that followed

tuples.episode_object: Drusus the Elder, the general who pushed to a great northern river and died on the way back
tuples.time_place_scope: the Rhine and the German interior
tuples.mechanism: the campaign of conquest that establishes a frontier by failing to cross it permanently
tuples.evidence_lens: marching camp archaeology and later campaign narratives

tuples.episode_object: Agrippina the Elder, the widow who carried her husband's ashes home as an accusation
tuples.time_place_scope: the Rhine frontier, Rome, and an island of exile
tuples.mechanism: the mourning widow as an opposition figure, and the exile that neutralises her
tuples.evidence_lens: narrative histories and the record of her sons' fates

tuples.episode_object: Agrippina the Younger, the empress who put a son on the throne and was killed by him
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the coastal villas in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the mother-regent whose usefulness expires when the son reaches maturity
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile histories, coin portraits showing her beside the emperor, and her lost memoirs

tuples.episode_object: Sejanus, the guard prefect who concentrated the cohorts in one camp and nearly took the state
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the guard barracks in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the concentration of a scattered guard into a single camp, which created a permanent political actor
tuples.evidence_lens: a senatorial history, inscriptions erased after his fall, and the camp's remains

tuples.episode_object: Messalina, the young empress destroyed by a marriage ceremony nobody can fully explain
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the imperial gardens in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the court faction fight decided by controlling access to a distracted ruler
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile narrative accounts and the systematic erasure of her name from inscriptions

tuples.episode_object: Britannicus, the son passed over for a stepson and dead at a dinner
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the displaced natural heir, whose survival is incompatible with an adopted successor
tuples.evidence_lens: narrative accounts of the death and the adoption documents implied by coinage

tuples.episode_object: Julia the Elder, the emperor's only child, exiled by her father under his own morality law
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and a prison island
tuples.mechanism: the dynastic marriage sequence, in which a daughter is married three times to make heirs
tuples.evidence_lens: the text of the marriage legislation and the record of her exile

tuples.episode_object: Antonia the Younger, the widow who refused remarriage and ran a household of client kings
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the eastern client courts
tuples.mechanism: the imperial household as a finishing school for foreign princes held as guests
tuples.evidence_lens: correspondence preserved in a Jewish historian's work, and estate records

tuples.episode_object: Tiberius Gemellus, the co-heir removed within a year of the will being read
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the divided testamentary inheritance, which a single successor resolves by elimination
tuples.evidence_lens: the terms of the will as reported and the coin record's silence

tuples.episode_object: Octavia the Younger, the sister married to a rival to seal a treaty that failed
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome, Greece, and the eastern provinces
tuples.mechanism: the marriage treaty between warlords, and the repudiation that functions as a declaration of war
tuples.evidence_lens: the treaty terms in later histories and contemporary political propaganda

tuples.episode_object: Poppaea Sabina, the empress whose funeral used a year's supply of eastern incense
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the imperial estates in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the consumption economy of a court, in which a funeral is a measurable commodity event
tuples.evidence_lens: a natural history's note on the incense, and coin portraiture

tuples.episode_object: Agrippa Postumus, the grandson exiled to an island and killed the week the old emperor died
tuples.time_place_scope: a small Italian island and Rome
tuples.mechanism: the tidying of the succession in the first hours of a new reign
tuples.evidence_lens: narrative accounts disagreeing about who gave the order

tuples.episode_object: Vespasian, the tax collector's son who won a civil war from a granary province
tuples.time_place_scope: Egypt, the Levant, and Italy in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the control of grain shipping as a decisive lever in a civil war fought over a city that had to eat
tuples.evidence_lens: a foreign historian's eyewitness narrative and coin issues from eastern mints

tuples.episode_object: Titus, the heir who commanded a siege and then spent his short reign on disasters
tuples.time_place_scope: the Levant, Rome, and the Bay of Naples
tuples.mechanism: imperial disaster relief as a governing performance, funded from the emperor's own purse
tuples.evidence_lens: eyewitness letters on a volcanic eruption and relief inscriptions

tuples.episode_object: Domitian, the younger son who ran the empire efficiently and was hated by the people who wrote
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome, the Danube, and the German frontier
tuples.mechanism: the tension between an efficient autocracy and a senatorial class that records its own humiliation
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile senatorial histories set against frontier archaeology and coin fineness

tuples.episode_object: Nerva, the elderly compromise chosen by the men who had just killed his predecessor
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome in the late first century
tuples.mechanism: the caretaker emperor who buys stability by adopting a general the army will accept
tuples.evidence_lens: the adoption announcement on coins and a brief panegyric tradition

tuples.episode_object: Trajan, the provincial soldier whose wars paid for a forum and a column to explain them
tuples.time_place_scope: the Danube, Mesopotamia, and Rome
tuples.mechanism: conquest financed by a captured gold region, and the public works that convert plunder into consent
tuples.evidence_lens: a carved narrative column, mining archaeology, and a governor's correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Hadrian, the emperor who gave back provinces and built walls instead
tuples.time_place_scope: Britain, the Rhine, the Danube, and the eastern provinces
tuples.mechanism: the deliberate strategic contraction, fixing a frontier line rather than pushing it
tuples.evidence_lens: a surviving frontier wall, an imperial travel itinerary from inscriptions, and coin series of provinces

tuples.episode_object: Antoninus Pius, the emperor who never left Italy and left almost no narrative behind
tuples.time_place_scope: Italy and the provinces governed by letter
tuples.mechanism: the administrative reign, whose evidence is legal rescripts rather than campaigns
tuples.evidence_lens: legal rescripts preserved in later codes and a dense inscriptional record

tuples.episode_object: Marcus Aurelius, the emperor who wrote private notes while fighting on a frozen frontier
tuples.time_place_scope: the Danube frontier and Rome in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the emperor's private philosophical journal as a coping instrument, never meant to be read
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving notebooks, a correspondence with a tutor, and campaign column reliefs

tuples.episode_object: Lucius Verus, the co-emperor whose eastern war brought back a plague
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern provinces and Rome
tuples.mechanism: formal collegial rule between two adopted brothers, and the epidemiology of a returning army
tuples.evidence_lens: joint coin issues and mortality evidence in inscriptions and papyri

tuples.episode_object: Commodus, the son who fought in an arena and renamed the months after himself
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the Danube in the later second century
tuples.mechanism: the hereditary succession that ends a run of adoptions, and the court conspiracy it invites
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile biographies, arena-themed coinage, and a colossal statue's recutting

tuples.episode_object: Faustina the Younger, the empress who travelled with the army
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern and Danubian campaigns in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the title of mother of the camp, an honorific that acknowledged a real presence on campaign
tuples.evidence_lens: coin legends granting the title and campaign correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Vitellius, the governor proclaimed by the Rhine legions in a year of four emperors
tuples.time_place_scope: the Rhine, northern Italy, and Rome in a single year
tuples.mechanism: the legionary proclamation, which showed that armies could make an emperor anywhere
tuples.evidence_lens: a compressed narrative of the civil war and mint output from provincial cities

tuples.episode_object: Otho, the emperor who ruled three months and ended a battle by taking his own life
tuples.time_place_scope: northern Italy in a single year
tuples.mechanism: the decision to stop a civil war by removing its cause, treated by contemporaries as unusual
tuples.evidence_lens: narrative accounts and coin issues from a very short reign

tuples.episode_object: Galba, the elderly governor who arrived in the city and refused to pay the guard
tuples.time_place_scope: Spain, Gaul, and Rome in a single year
tuples.mechanism: the unpaid donative, which turned the guard that made an emperor into the guard that killed him
tuples.evidence_lens: contemporary historians and the record of the guard's rapid change of allegiance

tuples.episode_object: Sabina, the empress whose marriage was politically necessary and personally reported as cold
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the travelling court in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the dynastic marriage that produces no heir, and the adoption machinery that fills the gap
tuples.evidence_lens: coin portraits, deification issues, and hostile biographical anecdote

tuples.episode_object: Aelius Caesar, the first chosen heir who died before his adoptive father
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the Danube in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the failed adoption, and the second choice that redefines a dynasty
tuples.evidence_lens: coin issues struck for a designated heir who never reigned

tuples.episode_object: Plotina, the empress credited by rumour with arranging a succession
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern provinces and Rome in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the deathbed adoption announced by the household, and the doubt it permanently attracts
tuples.evidence_lens: the announcement's timing in coin and inscriptional evidence, and later hostile accounts

tuples.episode_object: Avidius Cassius, the eastern general proclaimed emperor on a false report of a death
tuples.time_place_scope: Syria and Egypt in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the usurpation launched on bad news, which collapses when the news proves wrong
tuples.evidence_lens: provincial documents dated by his brief claim and later narrative accounts

tuples.episode_object: Domitia Longina, the empress who survived her husband's assassination and lived on for decades
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the imperial estates
tuples.mechanism: the survival of an imperial widow after a damned reign, and the estates that made it possible
tuples.evidence_lens: brick stamps from her estates and later inscriptions

tuples.episode_object: Titus Flavius Clemens, the imperial cousin executed for a charge nobody explains clearly
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome at the end of the first century
tuples.mechanism: the treason charge whose real content is hidden by the vagueness of the surviving record
tuples.evidence_lens: a terse notice in a historian and later confessional traditions claiming him

tuples.episode_object: Septimius Severus, the African senator who won a civil war and doubled the army's pay
tuples.time_place_scope: the Danube, Rome, Mesopotamia, and northern Britain
tuples.mechanism: the militarisation of the succession, funded by debasing the coinage to pay the legions
tuples.evidence_lens: silver fineness measurements, campaign inscriptions, and a frontier wall's rebuilding

tuples.episode_object: Julia Domna, the empress who ran the correspondence while her son ran the wars
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome, Syria, and the northern campaigns
tuples.mechanism: the empress as chief of the imperial secretariat, an office no law recognised
tuples.evidence_lens: her titles on inscriptions and the household staff recorded on tombstones

tuples.episode_object: Caracalla, the emperor who made everyone a citizen and taxed the new citizens
tuples.time_place_scope: the whole empire, the Rhine, and Mesopotamia
tuples.mechanism: universal citizenship as a fiscal measure, widening the base of the inheritance tax
tuples.evidence_lens: a papyrus copy of the edict and inheritance tax rates

tuples.episode_object: Geta, the co-emperor erased from a family portrait after his brother killed him
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome and the Egyptian provinces
tuples.mechanism: the formal erasure of memory, executed literally on painted panels and inscriptions
tuples.evidence_lens: a painted family tondo with one face scraped out, and chiselled inscriptions

tuples.episode_object: Macrinus, the guard prefect who became emperor without ever entering the senate house as one
tuples.time_place_scope: Syria and Anatolia in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the equestrian emperor, whose lack of senatorial rank made him easy to replace
tuples.evidence_lens: coin issues from eastern mints and a contemporary senator's history

tuples.episode_object: Elagabalus, the teenage priest who brought a black stone to Rome and made it the chief god
tuples.time_place_scope: Syria and Rome in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the imposition of a provincial cult at the centre, and the priesthood displaced by it
tuples.evidence_lens: a purpose-built temple, coin iconography of the stone, and hostile histories

tuples.episode_object: Julia Maesa, the grandmother who put two teenage emperors on the throne in four years
tuples.time_place_scope: Syria and Rome in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the dynastic grandmother as kingmaker, using an army's pay and a family resemblance
tuples.evidence_lens: coin portraits, senate honours, and a contemporary historian's account

tuples.episode_object: Severus Alexander, the young emperor killed with his mother in a camp mutiny
tuples.time_place_scope: the Rhine frontier in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the negotiated peace that a field army reads as cowardice, and the mutiny that follows
tuples.evidence_lens: a contemporary historian's narrative and the collapse of coin issues

tuples.episode_object: Maximinus Thrax, the giant soldier who never visited the city he ruled
tuples.time_place_scope: the Danube and northern Italy in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the soldier emperor who governs entirely from the field and never seeks civic legitimacy
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign inscriptions and the record of a senate that declared him an enemy

tuples.episode_object: Gordian the First, the elderly proconsul proclaimed in Africa and dead in three weeks
tuples.time_place_scope: the African province in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the provincial tax revolt that produces an accidental emperor
tuples.evidence_lens: a brief coin issue and later biographical compilations

tuples.episode_object: Philip the Arab, the emperor who paid a steppe power to go away and celebrated a millennium
tuples.time_place_scope: Mesopotamia and Rome in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the subsidy treaty, buying a frontier's quiet with an annual payment
tuples.evidence_lens: treaty terms in eastern sources and a millennial games issue on coins

tuples.episode_object: Decius, the emperor who required everyone to sacrifice and got a receipt system instead
tuples.time_place_scope: the whole empire and the Danube in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the empire-wide sacrifice order, administered by issuing certificates of compliance
tuples.evidence_lens: surviving papyrus certificates from Egyptian villages

tuples.episode_object: Valerian, the emperor captured alive by a rival empire and never returned
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern frontier in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the captured ruler, whose survival in enemy hands is worse for a state than his death
tuples.evidence_lens: a rival king's triumphal reliefs and inscriptions naming him

tuples.episode_object: Gallienus, the emperor who lost two thirds of the empire and reformed the cavalry
tuples.time_place_scope: the Rhine, the Danube, and Italy in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the mobile cavalry reserve, an answer to frontiers too long to hold everywhere at once
tuples.evidence_lens: coin reforms, unit histories in inscriptions, and hostile senatorial sources

tuples.episode_object: Postumus, the commander who founded a breakaway western empire that lasted fourteen years
tuples.time_place_scope: Gaul, Britain, and Spain in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the regional empire, complete with its own consuls and coinage, formed to defend one frontier
tuples.evidence_lens: a full parallel coin series and civic inscriptions naming his consulships

tuples.episode_object: Zenobia, the queen of a caravan city who ruled from Egypt to Anatolia
tuples.time_place_scope: the Syrian desert, Egypt, and Anatolia in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the caravan city's conversion of trade wealth and desert cavalry into an empire
tuples.evidence_lens: her coinage claiming imperial titles, and the ruins of her capital

tuples.episode_object: Aurelian, the emperor who reunited three empires in five years and walled the capital
tuples.time_place_scope: the Danube, the east, Gaul, and Rome
tuples.mechanism: the reconquest sequence, taking the wealthy east before the militarised west
tuples.evidence_lens: a surviving city wall, coin reform edicts, and campaign inscriptions

tuples.episode_object: Diocletian, the emperor who split the office four ways and then retired to grow cabbages
tuples.time_place_scope: the whole empire, the Danube, and a coastal palace
tuples.mechanism: the tetrarchy, an attempt to make succession a matter of appointment rather than of armies
tuples.evidence_lens: a price edict on stone, a surviving retirement palace, and the tetrarchic portrait style

tuples.episode_object: Carausius, the fleet commander who ruled Britain for seven years and issued excellent coins
tuples.time_place_scope: Britain and the Channel coast in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the naval usurpation, made possible by control of a sea a rival cannot cross unopposed
tuples.evidence_lens: his own high-quality coinage and coastal fort archaeology

tuples.episode_object: Claudius Gothicus, the emperor who won one great battle and died of plague in a year
tuples.time_place_scope: the Balkans in the third century
tuples.mechanism: the posthumous ancestor, claimed later by a dynasty that needed a respectable founder
tuples.evidence_lens: a later dynasty's genealogical claims and contemporary battle notices

coverage_profiles.subject: late Roman emperors of the West

tuples.episode_object: Constantine the First, the emperor who moved a capital east and changed a religion's legal status
tuples.time_place_scope: Britain, the Rhine, Italy, and the Bosphorus in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the legalisation and endowment of a church, which converted a persecuted body into a landowner
tuples.evidence_lens: a court biography, surviving legislation, and a new capital's foundation record

tuples.episode_object: Constantius the Second, the son who spent a reign fighting relatives and a frontier
tuples.time_place_scope: the Danube, Gaul, and the eastern frontier
tuples.mechanism: the dynastic massacre that clears a succession, and the cousins it leaves alive
tuples.evidence_lens: a contemporary soldier's history and church council records

tuples.episode_object: Julian, the philosopher emperor who tried to reverse a religious settlement in twenty months
tuples.time_place_scope: Gaul, Constantinople, and Mesopotamia in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the attempt to rebuild a displaced state religion as an organised institution
tuples.evidence_lens: his own surviving letters and treatises, and a soldier-historian's account

tuples.episode_object: Valentinian the First, the emperor who fortified a frontier and died in a rage at an embassy
tuples.time_place_scope: the Rhine and Danube frontiers in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the frontier building programme as strategy, replacing offensive campaigns with fortifications
tuples.evidence_lens: a dense series of frontier forts and a contemporary history

tuples.episode_object: Valens, the emperor who lost an army and his life to a people he had admitted
tuples.time_place_scope: the lower Danube and Thrace in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the mismanaged admission of a displaced people, and the revolt that follows a supply failure
tuples.evidence_lens: a contemporary historian's detailed account and Balkan destruction evidence

tuples.episode_object: Gratian, the young emperor who gave up an ancient priestly title and lost the west

tuples.mechanism: the renunciation of a traditional religious office by the ruler, and the political signal it sent
tuples.evidence_lens: legislation removing an altar from the senate house and a surviving exchange of pleas

tuples.episode_object: Theodosius the First, the last emperor to rule both halves and the one who split them for good
tuples.time_place_scope: the Balkans, Italy, and the eastern capital
tuples.mechanism: the settlement of a whole people inside the frontier as federate troops under their own leaders
tuples.evidence_lens: treaty terms in later summaries and legal codes on federate obligations

tuples.episode_object: Honorius, the emperor who was at a safe marsh capital when the old capital was sacked
tuples.time_place_scope: northern Italy and the Adriatic marshes in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the relocation of a court to an unassailable site, and the abandonment of the field that follows
tuples.evidence_lens: a defensible capital's archaeology and letters describing the sack

tuples.episode_object: Galla Placidia, the princess taken as a hostage, married to a king, and returned as a regent
tuples.time_place_scope: Italy, Gaul, and Spain in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the royal hostage marriage, which converts a captive into a diplomatic channel
tuples.evidence_lens: her building patronage, coin issues as regent, and contemporary chronicles

tuples.episode_object: Valentinian the Third, the emperor who killed his best general with his own hand
tuples.time_place_scope: Italy and the Gallic provinces in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the emperor and the patrician general, an unstable pairing where the soldier holds the real power
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicles, a surviving law code compiled in his name, and papal correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Majorian, the last western emperor to attempt a serious reconquest
tuples.time_place_scope: Gaul, Spain, and the western Mediterranean in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the fleet built for an African campaign, and the betrayal that destroys it before it sails
tuples.evidence_lens: his surviving legislation and a contemporary poet's panegyric

tuples.episode_object: Romulus Augustulus, the boy deposed without being killed, ending a line by anticlimax
tuples.time_place_scope: northern Italy in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the quiet abolition of an office, when a commander decides he does not need a figurehead
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle notices and the record of an eastern court's response

tuples.episode_object: Julius Nepos, the legitimate emperor who kept the title from a Dalmatian coast for five more years
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern Adriatic coast in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the rump legitimacy recognised abroad while another power holds the territory
tuples.evidence_lens: eastern recognition in chronicles and coin issues from a coastal mint

tuples.episode_object: Magnus Maximus, the British commander proclaimed by his troops and briefly recognised
tuples.time_place_scope: Britain, Gaul, and Italy in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the island garrison's proclamation, which strips a province to fund a continental claim
tuples.evidence_lens: coin issues, a British troop withdrawal in the archaeology, and church correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Constantine the Third, another British usurper who took Gaul and lost his son
tuples.time_place_scope: Britain, Gaul, and Spain in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the usurper who becomes briefly indispensable because he is the only defence available
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicles and the record of a formal recognition later withdrawn

tuples.episode_object: Eugenius, the schoolmaster made emperor by a general and defeated at a river
tuples.time_place_scope: Italy and the eastern Alps in the fourth century
tuples.mechanism: the figurehead emperor chosen for respectability by the soldier who actually decides
tuples.evidence_lens: battle accounts, and religious framing of the campaign by later church writers

tuples.episode_object: Petronius Maximus, the senator who arranged a murder and was stoned in the street
tuples.time_place_scope: Rome in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the senatorial coup that fails because the city population, not the senate, decides
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle accounts of the sack that followed within weeks

tuples.episode_object: Avitus, the Gallic aristocrat made emperor by a foreign king's endorsement
tuples.time_place_scope: Gaul and Italy in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the emperor sponsored by a federate kingdom, and the Italian resentment that unseats him
tuples.evidence_lens: a son-in-law's poems and letters, and Italian chronicle hostility

tuples.episode_object: Anthemius, the eastern nominee sent west with a fleet and a marriage
tuples.time_place_scope: Italy and the western Mediterranean in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the eastern intervention, funding a western reconquest that fails at sea
tuples.evidence_lens: eastern chronicle accounts of expedition costs and a western panegyric

tuples.episode_object: Glycerius, the emperor deposed and made a bishop instead of a corpse
tuples.time_place_scope: northern Italy and the Adriatic in the fifth century
tuples.mechanism: the ecclesiastical retirement, a way of removing a claimant without creating a martyr
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle notices and episcopal lists

tuples.episode_object: Justinian the First, the emperor who codified the law and reconquered two coasts he could not hold
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern capital, North Africa, and Italy in the sixth century
tuples.mechanism: the legal codification that outlived the reconquest, turning centuries of rulings into one book
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving law compilation, a court historian's public and private accounts, and church building

tuples.episode_object: Theodora, the empress from the hippodrome who told a court not to run
