tuples.mechanism: the imperial consort as a decisive voice in council, recorded by a hostile insider
tuples.evidence_lens: a court historian's two contradictory works and mosaic portraiture

tuples.episode_object: Heraclius, the emperor who lost the east twice and reorganised what was left
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern capital, Anatolia, and Mesopotamia in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the conversion of an army into a settled provincial militia when cash revenue collapses
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign accounts, seal evidence for new provinces, and coin weight reductions

tuples.episode_object: Leo the Third, the emperor who stopped an arms-length siege and started an argument about images
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and Anatolia in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the state-driven religious controversy, in which imperial policy divides an empire's own clergy
tuples.evidence_lens: hostile monastic chronicles, coin iconography changes, and later council acts

tuples.episode_object: Irene, the empress who blinded her own son and reigned as emperor in her own name
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the Anatolian provinces in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the female sole ruler using the male title, and the succession problem her sex created abroad
tuples.evidence_lens: her coins using the male imperial title, and council records

tuples.episode_object: Basil the First, the peasant groom who murdered his patron and founded a long dynasty
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the eastern frontier in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the court favourite's rise through the stables and the bedchamber to the throne
tuples.evidence_lens: a grandson's flattering biography read against other chronicle traditions

tuples.episode_object: Constantine the Seventh, the scholar emperor who wrote handbooks while others governed
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the reign spent as a nominal senior while regents and colleagues rule, and the books it produced
tuples.evidence_lens: his own surviving administrative and ceremonial treatises

tuples.episode_object: Nikephoros the Second, the ascetic general who took a throne and a widow with it
tuples.time_place_scope: Crete, Syria, and the capital in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the marriage to a predecessor's widow as a legitimating device, and the murder that ends it
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign histories and a foreign envoy's hostile report of the court

tuples.episode_object: John the First, the general who killed his cousin and then governed better than him
tuples.time_place_scope: the Balkans and Syria in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the usurpation followed by public penance, which converts a murder into a reign
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicles, and the record of a church-imposed penance

tuples.episode_object: Basil the Second, the emperor who spent fifty years on campaign and left a full treasury
tuples.time_place_scope: the Balkans, Anatolia, and the Caucasus
tuples.mechanism: the sustained attrition campaign, financed by taxing great estates rather than by borrowing
tuples.evidence_lens: legislation against the powerful, campaign chronicles, and treasury figures reported at his death

tuples.episode_object: Zoe, the empress who transmitted a throne through three husbands and an adoption
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: legitimacy carried by a woman of the ruling house and conferred on the men she married
tuples.evidence_lens: a court insider's memoirs and mosaic portraits with recut faces

tuples.episode_object: Romanos the Fourth, the emperor captured in a battle and blinded by his own side
tuples.time_place_scope: eastern Anatolia in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the defeat whose political consequences at home exceed its military ones on the field
tuples.evidence_lens: the accounts of two rival court traditions and the loss of Anatolian seals

tuples.episode_object: Alexios the First, the general who stabilised a collapsing state by marriage and devaluation
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital, the Balkans, and Anatolia in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the family-based state, in which imperial kin hold the great offices as a single interest group
tuples.evidence_lens: a daughter's long history of his reign and a reformed coinage

tuples.episode_object: Anna Komnene, the princess who lost a succession and wrote the history instead
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and a monastery in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the failed female claim, and the historiographical settling of accounts that followed
tuples.evidence_lens: her own long history and the conventual records of her later life

tuples.episode_object: Manuel the First, the emperor who spent a treasury on the west and lost a pass in the east
tuples.time_place_scope: the Balkans, Italy, and Anatolia in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the two-front foreign policy, which buys western allies with subsidies it cannot sustain
tuples.evidence_lens: treaty texts, western chronicles, and the coin fineness record

tuples.episode_object: Andronikos the First, the elderly cousin who took power on a wave of popular anger
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the populist purge of a court, and the mob that destroys the man it made
tuples.evidence_lens: a hostile contemporary historian who witnessed the events

tuples.episode_object: Michael the Eighth, the regent who blinded a boy emperor and retook a lost capital
tuples.time_place_scope: a western Anatolian exile court and the recovered capital in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the government in exile that reconquers its own capital and must then legitimise the interim
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicles from two rival successor states and church excommunication records

tuples.episode_object: John the Sixth, the emperor who wrote his own history of the civil war he fought
tuples.time_place_scope: the Balkans and the capital in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the civil war between a regency and a chief minister, fought with foreign mercenaries by both sides
tuples.evidence_lens: his own memoirs read against a rival emperor's history

tuples.episode_object: Manuel the Second, the emperor who toured western courts asking for help
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital, Italy, France, and England around the turn of the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the diplomatic tour as a last instrument, trading theological concessions for troops that never came
tuples.evidence_lens: his own letters, western court records, and a surviving portrait

tuples.episode_object: Constantine the Eleventh, the last emperor, who died in a breach and left no body to bury
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital during a siege in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the final siege in which artillery makes a great wall obsolete
tuples.evidence_lens: eyewitness siege diaries from both sides and the archaeology of the breached walls

tuples.episode_object: Clovis the First, the war leader whose baptism turned a warband into a kingdom
tuples.time_place_scope: northern Gaul and the Rhine valley at the turn of the sixth century
tuples.mechanism: conversion to the same faith as the conquered population, which bought bishops as administrators
tuples.evidence_lens: a bishop's history written a lifetime later, and a surviving law code

tuples.episode_object: Chlothar the First, the son who outlived his brothers and reunited a divided inheritance
tuples.time_place_scope: Gaul and the Rhineland in the sixth century
tuples.mechanism: partible inheritance among sons, which guarantees a war and occasionally a reunification
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicles, charters, and the geography of the partitions

tuples.episode_object: Brunhilda, the queen who governed for forty years and was executed by being dragged behind a horse
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern Frankish kingdoms in the sixth and seventh centuries
tuples.mechanism: the long dowager regency, and the aristocratic revolt it eventually provokes
tuples.evidence_lens: a hostile chronicle tradition, papal correspondence, and her road and church building

tuples.episode_object: Fredegund, the queen whose feud with a rival shaped two generations of policy
tuples.time_place_scope: the western Frankish kingdoms in the sixth century
tuples.mechanism: the royal feud as an organising principle of politics, absorbing bishops and dukes into two camps
tuples.evidence_lens: a contemporary bishop's history and later chronicle compilations

tuples.episode_object: Dagobert the First, the last Merovingian to govern rather than to be governed
tuples.time_place_scope: Gaul, the Rhine, and the Slav frontier in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the itinerant court, which taxed by eating its way around its own estates
tuples.evidence_lens: charters granted at named estates, and a royal abbey's foundation records

tuples.episode_object: Charles Martel, the mayor of the palace who ruled without a crown

tuples.mechanism: the household office that absorbs royal power while leaving the royal title in place
tuples.evidence_lens: annals, charters issued in a king's name, and church land grants to soldiers

tuples.episode_object: Pepin the Short, the mayor who asked a pope whether the title should follow the power
tuples.time_place_scope: Gaul and Italy in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the papal ruling as a legitimating instrument, exchanged for military protection in Italy
tuples.evidence_lens: papal correspondence, annals, and a donation of Italian territory

tuples.episode_object: Charlemagne, the king crowned emperor by a pope who needed him more than he needed the title
tuples.time_place_scope: Gaul, Saxony, Italy, and the Spanish march across a long reign
tuples.mechanism: the revival of an imperial title in the west, and the eastern court that refused to recognise it
tuples.evidence_lens: a courtier's biography, capitularies, and a coinage reform

tuples.episode_object: Louis the Pious, the emperor who divided an empire, was deposed by his sons, and got it back

tuples.mechanism: the written succession plan that fails when new sons are born after it is signed
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving division ordinance, annals, and penitential accounts

tuples.episode_object: Lothar the First, the eldest son who kept the imperial title and the least defensible strip
tuples.time_place_scope: the middle kingdom from the North Sea to Italy in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the partition treaty that creates a long thin realm with no natural frontier
tuples.evidence_lens: the treaty text and later disputes over its middle territories

tuples.episode_object: Charles the Bald, the youngest son who out-negotiated his brothers for forty years
tuples.time_place_scope: western Francia and Italy in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the assembly capitulary, which bought aristocratic consent for defence against seaborne raiders
tuples.evidence_lens: capitularies on bridge building and fortification, and annals of raids

tuples.episode_object: Louis the German, the brother who built an eastern kingdom out of the same family quarrel
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern Frankish lands and the Slav frontier in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the oath sworn in two languages, which shows a single elite splitting into two
tuples.evidence_lens: the recorded text of an oath in two vernaculars, and eastern annals

tuples.episode_object: Charles the Fat, the emperor who briefly reunited the empire and was deposed for buying off a siege
tuples.time_place_scope: the whole Frankish world in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the payment made to lift a siege, read by the nobility as an abdication of the war leader's role
tuples.evidence_lens: a besieged city's verse account and deposition records

tuples.episode_object: Bertrada of Laon, the queen mother who arranged an Italian marriage her son later cancelled
tuples.time_place_scope: Francia and Lombard Italy in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the marriage alliance as foreign policy, and the repudiation that reverses it
tuples.evidence_lens: papal letters objecting to the match, and annals

tuples.episode_object: Judith of Bavaria, the second wife whose son's inheritance restarted a civil war
tuples.time_place_scope: the Frankish empire in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the second marriage that reopens a settled succession and splits a court
tuples.evidence_lens: partisan annals from three different sides of the same conflict

tuples.episode_object: Charles the Simple, the king who gave a river valley to a fleet commander and got a frontier
tuples.time_place_scope: northern Francia and the lower Seine in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the grant of land to seaborne raiders in exchange for defending the coast against others
tuples.evidence_lens: a later account of the agreement and the charter record of the new lordship

tuples.episode_object: Childeric the Third, the last of a line, deposed and tonsured in a monastery
tuples.time_place_scope: Francia in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the tonsure as political death, removing a claimant without killing him
tuples.evidence_lens: annals recording the deposition and the papal ruling that preceded it

tuples.episode_object: Carloman, the brother who resigned a share of power and entered a monastery
tuples.time_place_scope: Francia and Italy in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the voluntary retirement from rule, rare enough that chroniclers explain it at length
tuples.evidence_lens: annals and monastic records of his profession

tuples.episode_object: Pepin of Italy, the son who governed a sub-kingdom and predeceased his father
tuples.time_place_scope: Lombard Italy in the eighth and ninth centuries
tuples.mechanism: the sub-kingdom given to a son as an apprenticeship and a garrison command
tuples.evidence_lens: Italian capitularies issued in his name and annal entries

tuples.episode_object: Arnulf of Carinthia, the nephew who took an empire and could not hold Italy
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern Frankish lands and Italy in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the illegitimate claimant accepted because the legitimate one cannot defend the frontier
tuples.evidence_lens: eastern annals, coin issues, and Italian chronicle hostility

tuples.episode_object: Raedwald, the East Anglian king who kept two altars and may lie in a buried ship
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern coast and its river estuaries in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the hedged conversion, keeping an old cult and a new one in the same hall
tuples.evidence_lens: a monk's history recording the two altars, and a rich ship burial

tuples.episode_object: Edwin of Northumbria, the exile who returned with an army and converted on a debate
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern kingdoms and the eastern coast in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the royal council convened to decide a conversion, which made belief an act of policy
tuples.evidence_lens: a monastic history reporting the council speeches

tuples.episode_object: Oswald, the king killed in battle and dismembered into relics
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern kingdoms and the western march in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the making of a royal saint, in which relics distribute a dead king's authority across a country
tuples.evidence_lens: hagiography, church dedications, and the geography of relic claims

tuples.episode_object: Penda, the last great pagan king, who won more battles than the Christians who wrote about him
tuples.time_place_scope: the midland kingdoms in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the durable pagan kingship that survives by alliance rather than by conversion
tuples.evidence_lens: a hostile monastic history and the battle sites it names

tuples.episode_object: Offa of Mercia, the king who built a dyke and wrote to a foreign emperor as an equal
tuples.time_place_scope: the midlands and the Welsh march in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the earthwork frontier, which defines a border without needing to garrison it
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving dyke, a coinage in his name, and a letter exchange

tuples.episode_object: Alfred, the king who lost a kingdom to a winter raid and rebuilt it around fortified towns
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern kingdom and the marshes in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the burghal system, a network of fortified towns each supported by a measured stretch of countryside
tuples.evidence_lens: a survey listing the forts and their hides, a court biography, and town plans

tuples.episode_object: Aethelflaed, the ruler of the midlands who fortified a frontier for her brother
tuples.time_place_scope: the midland shires in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the woman ruling a kingdom under a title that avoided the word queen
tuples.evidence_lens: a midland chronicle register and the archaeology of her fortified towns

tuples.episode_object: Athelstan, the first king of all the English and an assiduous collector of relics
tuples.time_place_scope: the whole island and its northern frontier in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the great assembly, at which kings from across an island attended and were listed as witnesses
tuples.evidence_lens: charter witness lists, coin issues, and relic donation records

tuples.episode_object: Edgar, the king crowned twice, the second time as a carefully staged imperial rite
tuples.time_place_scope: the whole kingdom and a western river in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the delayed coronation, staged as a liturgical event once a reign is already secure
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving coronation order and monastic reform charters

tuples.episode_object: Aethelred the Unready, the king whose reign is measured in the payments he made to raiders
tuples.time_place_scope: the whole kingdom and the North Sea in the tenth and eleventh centuries
tuples.mechanism: the tribute levy, a national tax raised repeatedly to buy off a fleet
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle entries recording each payment, and vast coin hoards abroad

tuples.episode_object: Cnut, the conqueror who ruled three kingdoms and legislated like a native
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Denmark, and Norway in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the North Sea empire held together by a fleet, a household guard, and local law
tuples.evidence_lens: his law codes, a letter to the English people, and coin issues in three realms

tuples.episode_object: Emma of Normandy, the queen married to two kings and mother of two more
tuples.time_place_scope: England and Normandy across four reigns
tuples.mechanism: the queen as dynastic continuity across a conquest, valuable to both sides
tuples.evidence_lens: a work of praise commissioned by her, and charters naming her estates

tuples.episode_object: Edward the Confessor, the pious king whose childlessness set up a contested succession
tuples.time_place_scope: England and Normandy in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the unresolved succession, with three plausible claims and no settled law of inheritance
tuples.evidence_lens: a life commissioned by his queen, chronicle accounts, and later Norman justifications

tuples.episode_object: Harold Godwinson, the earl who was king for nine months and fought two invasions in three weeks
tuples.time_place_scope: the north and the south coast in a single year
tuples.mechanism: the forced march between two fronts, and what it costs an army before it fights
tuples.evidence_lens: an embroidered narrative hanging, chronicle accounts, and the battle terrain

tuples.episode_object: Edmund Ironside, the king who fought five battles in a year and agreed to a partition
tuples.time_place_scope: England in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the negotiated partition between two claimants, void the moment one of them dies
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle accounts of the campaigns and the terms

tuples.episode_object: Aethelbert of Kent, the first English king to have his laws written down
tuples.time_place_scope: the south-eastern kingdom in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the writing of customary law in the vernacular, a by-product of a new literate clergy
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving law text and a missionary's correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Oswiu, the king who chose one dating of a great festival and settled a church's alignment
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern kingdoms in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the synod as an instrument of royal policy, choosing between two ecclesiastical networks
tuples.evidence_lens: a monastic history's account of the synod's arguments

tuples.episode_object: Wulfhere of Mercia, the son of a pagan king who expanded a Christian kingdom southward
tuples.time_place_scope: the midlands and the south coast in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the client kingdom and the sub-king, a structure that let one dynasty rule beyond its own people
tuples.evidence_lens: charters naming sub-kings and a monastic history's genealogies

tuples.episode_object: Edward the Elder, the king who took the midlands by building forts one river at a time
tuples.time_place_scope: the midland rivers and the eastern shires in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the incremental fort campaign, advancing a frontier by construction rather than by battle
tuples.evidence_lens: a chronicle recording each fort and its year, and excavated burh defences

tuples.episode_object: Eadwig, the young king whose reign split a kingdom between two brothers in two years
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern kingdom in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the disputed accession resolved by partition along an old internal frontier
tuples.evidence_lens: charters showing a divided witness list and later monastic hostility

tuples.episode_object: William the First, the duke who won a kingdom in one afternoon and spent twenty years holding it
tuples.time_place_scope: Normandy, the south coast, and the north of England in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the castle-and-garrison occupation, which holds a country with a few hundred strongpoints
tuples.evidence_lens: a great land survey, castle earthworks, and both Norman and English chronicles

tuples.episode_object: William the Second, the king killed by an arrow in a forest nobody investigated
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern forests and the Norman frontier in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the hunting accident that is politically convenient, and the succession that moves within hours
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle accounts and the speed of the successor's ride to the treasury

tuples.episode_object: Henry the First, the youngest brother who seized a treasury before anyone could stop him
tuples.time_place_scope: England and Normandy at the turn of the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the accession charter of liberties, promising to end abuses in exchange for immediate recognition
tuples.evidence_lens: the charter text, exchequer records, and chronicle accounts

tuples.episode_object: Matilda, the empress who was never crowned and never stopped claiming
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Normandy, and Anjou in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the oath sworn to a female heir and abandoned as soon as it was tested
tuples.evidence_lens: charters issued as lady of the English, and partisan chronicles

tuples.episode_object: Stephen, the count who took a throne and lost the ability to govern it
tuples.time_place_scope: England and Normandy through a long civil war
tuples.mechanism: the breakdown of central justice during a disputed succession, and the private castles that fill the gap
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle descriptions of unlicensed castles and the treaty that ended the war

tuples.episode_object: Henry the Second, the king who governed from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees on horseback
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Normandy, Anjou, Aquitaine, and Ireland
tuples.mechanism: the itinerant justice system, sending royal judges on circuit so a king's law travels further than he does
tuples.evidence_lens: the pipe rolls, assize texts, and a treatise on the laws of the realm

tuples.episode_object: Eleanor of Aquitaine, the duchess who was queen of two kingdoms and imprisoned by the second
tuples.time_place_scope: Aquitaine, France, and England across the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the heiress whose duchy travels with her marriage, making her person a foreign policy
tuples.evidence_lens: her own charters, chronicles from both kingdoms, and her tomb effigy

tuples.episode_object: Richard the First, the king who spent six months of a ten-year reign in his kingdom
tuples.time_place_scope: Aquitaine, the Levant, and an Austrian prison
tuples.mechanism: the ransom levy, a tax on a whole kingdom to redeem one man from captivity
tuples.evidence_lens: exchequer records of the ransom collection and the terms of his release

tuples.episode_object: John, the king who lost a duchy, quarrelled with a pope, and signed a charter under duress
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Normandy, and a Thames meadow in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the baronial coalition that converts private grievance into a written constitutional document
tuples.evidence_lens: the charter's surviving exemplars, chancery rolls, and papal annulment

tuples.episode_object: Robert Curthose, the eldest son who inherited a duchy and spent twenty-eight years as a prisoner
tuples.time_place_scope: Normandy, the Levant, and an English castle
tuples.mechanism: the captive brother, kept alive because killing him would legitimise killing kings
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle accounts and the record of his long confinement

tuples.episode_object: William Adelin, the heir drowned in a Channel crossing that changed a succession
tuples.time_place_scope: the Norman coast in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the single accident that destroys a succession plan and produces a civil war a decade later
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle accounts of the wreck and the subsequent oath-taking

tuples.episode_object: Henry the Young King, the son crowned in his father's lifetime who rebelled anyway
tuples.time_place_scope: England and the French lands in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the associative coronation, meant to secure a succession and instead creating a rival court
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicles, and the charters issued by a king with no territory

tuples.episode_object: Adeliza of Louvain, the second queen whose childlessness redirected a dynasty
tuples.time_place_scope: England and the Low Countries in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the remarriage undertaken specifically for an heir, and the consequences when it fails
tuples.evidence_lens: charters, monastic patronage records, and chronicle commentary

tuples.episode_object: Geoffrey of Anjou, the count whose marriage joined two territories and whose badge named a dynasty
tuples.time_place_scope: Anjou and Normandy in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the conquest of a duchy on a wife's behalf, held in trust for a son
tuples.evidence_lens: Angevin chronicles and a surviving enamel funerary plaque

tuples.episode_object: Arthur of Brittany, the nephew with the better claim who vanished in a castle
tuples.time_place_scope: Brittany, Anjou, and the Seine valley in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the disappearance of a rival claimant, and the loss of an entire duchy's loyalty that follows
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle rumours, and the French court's use of the case in a forfeiture judgment

tuples.episode_object: Isabella of Angouleme, the child bride whose marriage triggered a war and a confiscation
tuples.time_place_scope: western France in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the feudal summons ignored, which lets an overlord declare lands forfeit
tuples.evidence_lens: the French court records of the forfeiture and chronicle accounts

tuples.episode_object: Ranulf Flambard, the bishop who ran a king's finances and escaped from a tower
tuples.time_place_scope: England and Normandy at the turn of the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the clerical treasurer, whose expertise makes him indispensable and hated in equal measure
tuples.evidence_lens: exchequer practice described in later treatises and hostile monastic chronicles

tuples.episode_object: Thomas Becket, the chancellor who became an archbishop and stopped agreeing with the king
tuples.time_place_scope: England, France, and a cathedral in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the conflict between royal and church courts over who may try a criminous clerk
tuples.evidence_lens: the constitutions at issue, letter collections, and the pilgrimage record after the murder

tuples.episode_object: Hubert Walter, the archbishop who governed a kingdom while its king was abroad
tuples.time_place_scope: England during the crusading and ransom years
tuples.mechanism: the justiciar, an office that lets a kingdom function without its king for years at a time
tuples.evidence_lens: chancery rolls begun under his administration and chronicle assessments

tuples.episode_object: William Marshal, the knight who served five kings and ended as regent for a boy
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Normandy, and the tournament circuit
tuples.mechanism: the household knight's rise by loyalty and marriage into the highest office in a kingdom
tuples.evidence_lens: a verse biography commissioned by his family, and charter witness lists

tuples.episode_object: Henry the Third, the boy king whose long reign produced a parliament and a rebellion
tuples.time_place_scope: England and Gascony across a very long thirteenth-century reign
tuples.mechanism: the minority council, which institutionalises government by a group and never fully hands it back
tuples.evidence_lens: chancery rolls, the provisions agreed and repudiated, and chronicle accounts

tuples.episode_object: Edward the First, the king who codified law, expelled a community, and built a ring of castles
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Wales, and Scotland in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the castle-building programme as conquest infrastructure, costed in surviving accounts
tuples.evidence_lens: detailed building accounts, statutes, and the castles themselves

tuples.episode_object: Edward the Second, the king deposed by a parliament and his own wife
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Scotland, and a Gloucestershire castle in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the formal deposition by assembly, which had to invent a procedure as it went
tuples.evidence_lens: the articles of deposition and chronicle accounts of the ceremony

tuples.episode_object: Isabella of France, the queen who invaded her husband's kingdom with a small force and won
tuples.time_place_scope: France, the eastern counties, and the Welsh march in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the invasion that succeeds because nobody defends an unpopular regime
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle narratives, and the household accounts of her expedition

tuples.episode_object: Edward the Third, the king who claimed a foreign crown and started a very long war
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Flanders, and northern France in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the claim through a female line, advanced to justify a war and denied by a rival succession law
tuples.evidence_lens: the diplomatic claim documents and parliamentary war taxation rolls

tuples.episode_object: The Black Prince, the heir who won two great battles and died before his father
tuples.time_place_scope: France, Spain, and Aquitaine in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the profitable campaign of destruction, funded by ransoms and plunder rather than by taxation
tuples.evidence_lens: ransom records, chevauchee itineraries, and his own register

tuples.episode_object: Richard the Second, the boy who faced a rising in person and lost his throne twenty years later
tuples.time_place_scope: London, Ireland, and the north in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the royal claim to unrestrained authority, and the aristocratic coalition it unites against him
tuples.evidence_lens: parliamentary rolls, chronicle accounts, and a commissioned portrait

tuples.episode_object: Henry the Fourth, the usurper who spent his reign putting down the men who had helped him
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Wales, and the north in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the usurpation that legitimises further usurpation, and the rebellions that follow
tuples.evidence_lens: the parliamentary record of the accession and rebellion trial records

tuples.episode_object: Henry the Fifth, the king who won a famous battle and died of camp sickness at thirty-five
tuples.time_place_scope: Normandy and the Seine valley in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the siege war of attrition behind the famous battle, and the treaty that made a French heir
tuples.evidence_lens: siege accounts, the treaty text, and financial records of the garrisons

tuples.episode_object: Henry the Sixth, the king crowned in two countries as a child and unfit to rule either
tuples.time_place_scope: England, Normandy, and the midlands in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the incapable adult king, around whom a court party and a protectorate compete
tuples.evidence_lens: council minutes recording his illness and the protectorate arrangements

tuples.episode_object: Margaret of Anjou, the queen who led an army because her husband could not
tuples.time_place_scope: the midlands, the north, and France in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the queen consort as war leader when the crown's authority has no other body to occupy
tuples.evidence_lens: her letters, chronicle accounts, and attainder records

tuples.episode_object: Richard of York, the claimant who was offered a succession and killed before he could take it
tuples.time_place_scope: Ireland, London, and the north in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the negotiated act of accord, disinheriting a living heir and guaranteeing a war
tuples.evidence_lens: the parliamentary act itself and the campaign records that followed

tuples.episode_object: Edward the Fourth, the king who won a throne at eighteen, lost it, and won it again
tuples.time_place_scope: the midlands, the north, and the Low Countries
tuples.mechanism: the exile and return, financed by a foreign ruler with an interest in the outcome
tuples.evidence_lens: a contemporary account of the return campaign and continental diplomatic records

tuples.episode_object: Warwick the Kingmaker, the earl who made two kings and died fighting the first
tuples.time_place_scope: the midlands, Calais, and France in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the overmighty subject, whose private retinue rivals a royal army
tuples.evidence_lens: retainer indentures, chronicle accounts, and estate valuations

tuples.episode_object: Elizabeth Woodville, the widow whose secret marriage split a court
tuples.time_place_scope: England in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the marriage outside the diplomatic market, which wastes a king's most valuable asset
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle accounts of the announcement and the grants to her family

tuples.episode_object: Richard the Third, the protector who took a throne and lost it in two years
tuples.time_place_scope: the north, London, and a midland field in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the protectorship converted into a claim by declaring a marriage invalid
tuples.evidence_lens: the parliamentary act setting out the claim, and the archaeology of his burial

tuples.episode_object: The princes in the Tower, the two boys whose fate is the most argued gap in the record
tuples.time_place_scope: London in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the absence of evidence as a political fact, which every later regime found useful
tuples.evidence_lens: contemporary silence, later hostile accounts, and disputed physical remains

tuples.episode_object: Henry the Seventh, the exile with a thin claim who won a battle and married the other side
tuples.time_place_scope: Brittany, Wales, and England in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the marriage that ends a dynastic war by merging two claims into one heir
tuples.evidence_lens: the act of settlement, financial records of a tight-fisted reign, and pretender trials

tuples.episode_object: Perkin Warbeck, the pretender who claimed to be a prince and was received by two courts
tuples.time_place_scope: Flanders, Scotland, Ireland, and England in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the foreign-sponsored pretender, useful to neighbours as leverage rather than as a candidate
tuples.evidence_lens: diplomatic correspondence, a confession of doubtful value, and trial records

tuples.episode_object: Lambert Simnel, the boy crowned in Ireland and later put to work in a royal kitchen
tuples.time_place_scope: Ireland and the midlands in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the clemency shown to a figurehead, which publicly demotes a rebellion to a fraud
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicle accounts of the coronation and household records of his later employment

coverage_profiles.subject: Capetian and Valois kings of France

tuples.episode_object: Hugh Capet, the duke elected king of a kingdom he barely controlled
tuples.time_place_scope: the Paris region and the Loire in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the elective monarchy converted to a hereditary one by crowning the heir in the father's lifetime
tuples.evidence_lens: charters, chronicle accounts of the election, and coronation records

tuples.episode_object: Philip the First, the king excommunicated for a marriage he refused to give up
tuples.time_place_scope: the royal domain in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the church's marriage jurisdiction used against a king, and the limits of that weapon
tuples.evidence_lens: papal and conciliar records, and royal charters continuing through the sentence

tuples.episode_object: Louis the Sixth, the king who spent a reign subduing castles within a day's ride of his capital
tuples.time_place_scope: the small royal domain in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the reduction of robber castles as the first step in building a state
tuples.evidence_lens: an abbot's biography of him and charters of confiscated lordships

tuples.episode_object: Louis the Seventh, the king whose divorce handed a duchy to a rival
tuples.time_place_scope: France, the Levant, and Aquitaine in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the annulment that returns an heiress and her lands to the marriage market
tuples.evidence_lens: conciliar annulment records and the immediate remarriage's consequences

tuples.episode_object: Philip the Second, the king who took Normandy in two years by using a court judgment
tuples.time_place_scope: Normandy, the Loire, and Flanders in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the feudal forfeiture, using the overlord's own court to strip a vassal of his lands
tuples.evidence_lens: the court record of the summons and the campaign accounts

tuples.episode_object: Louis the Eighth, the prince invited to take an English throne and later a southern crusade
tuples.time_place_scope: England and the Languedoc in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the invitation from foreign barons, which makes a claim without a dynastic basis
tuples.evidence_lens: chronicles from both kingdoms and the southern campaign records

tuples.episode_object: Blanche of Castile, the regent who governed twice and held a kingdom together
tuples.time_place_scope: France in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the queen regent whose authority rests on a dying king's testament rather than on custom
tuples.evidence_lens: her acts issued as regent and baronial correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Louis the Ninth, the king who arbitrated other kingdoms' disputes and died on a crusade
tuples.time_place_scope: France, Egypt, and North Africa in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the reputation for justice converted into an international arbitration role
tuples.evidence_lens: a companion's biography, enquiry records into royal officials, and canonisation files

tuples.episode_object: Philip the Fourth, the king who destroyed a military order and moved a papacy
tuples.time_place_scope: France, Flanders, and southern France at the turn of the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the state trial of a wealthy corporation, which converts a fiscal need into a heresy proceeding
tuples.evidence_lens: the trial records, coin debasement evidence, and papal correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Philip the Sixth, the first Valois king, chosen over a rival claim through a woman
tuples.time_place_scope: France and Flanders in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the exclusion of female-line claims, decided by an assembly and justified afterwards
tuples.evidence_lens: the assembly's decision, later legal treatises, and the war that followed

tuples.episode_object: John the Second, the king captured in battle and held for a ransom his country could not pay
tuples.time_place_scope: France, Poitou, and England in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the royal ransom, which mortgages a kingdom's revenue for a generation
tuples.evidence_lens: the treaty setting the sum and the tax records raised against it

tuples.episode_object: Charles the Fifth, the king who won a war by refusing to fight battles
tuples.time_place_scope: France in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the strategy of avoiding pitched battle while retaking fortresses one at a time
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign accounts, a commissioned history, and a royal library catalogue

tuples.episode_object: Charles the Sixth, the king whose recurring illness split a kingdom into two parties
tuples.time_place_scope: Paris and the provinces in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries
tuples.mechanism: the incapacity of a ruler with no legal mechanism for replacing him
tuples.evidence_lens: council registers, physicians' accounts, and partisan chronicles

tuples.episode_object: Isabeau of Bavaria, the queen blamed by later writers for a treaty she co-signed
tuples.time_place_scope: Paris and the Loire in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the treaty that disinherits a son, and the historiography that assigns the blame to a woman
tuples.evidence_lens: the treaty text and the later polemical tradition around her

tuples.episode_object: Charles the Seventh, the disinherited heir who was crowned in a cathedral he had to fight to reach
tuples.time_place_scope: the Loire, Reims, and Normandy in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the coronation as a legitimating act that must physically reach a particular church
tuples.evidence_lens: the coronation records, campaign accounts, and a rehabilitation trial

tuples.episode_object: Louis the Eleventh, the king who preferred bribery, spies, and treaties to battles
tuples.time_place_scope: France, Burgundy, and the Low Countries in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the pension diplomacy, which buys foreign nobles more cheaply than an army costs
tuples.evidence_lens: his surviving letters, treasury accounts of pensions, and hostile memoirs

tuples.episode_object: Charles the Eighth, the king who marched an army to Naples and started sixty years of Italian wars
tuples.time_place_scope: France and the Italian peninsula in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the dynastic claim to a distant throne, used to justify an expedition an army wants anyway
tuples.evidence_lens: campaign diaries, Italian chronicles, and the diplomatic league that followed

tuples.episode_object: Anne of Brittany, the duchess married to two successive kings to keep a duchy attached
tuples.time_place_scope: Brittany and France at the turn of the sixteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the marriage contract as an instrument of territorial union, with clauses for a widow's remarriage
tuples.evidence_lens: the marriage contracts themselves and ducal administrative records

tuples.episode_object: Francis the First, the king captured in Italy and ransomed with his own sons
tuples.time_place_scope: Italy, Spain, and France in the sixteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the exchange of royal children as hostages, a routine guarantee in early modern treaties
tuples.evidence_lens: the treaty terms, ambassadorial correspondence, and the boys' later accounts

tuples.episode_object: Catherine de Medici, the queen mother who governed through three sons and a religious war
tuples.time_place_scope: France across the later sixteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the mother regent balancing two armed confessions with edicts of limited toleration
tuples.evidence_lens: her voluminous correspondence, edicts of pacification, and hostile pamphlets

tuples.episode_object: Otto the First, the German king who revived an imperial title by rescuing a pope
tuples.time_place_scope: Saxony, Italy, and the Hungarian frontier in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the Italian expedition as the price of an imperial coronation, repeated by every successor
tuples.evidence_lens: a court chronicle, imperial diplomas, and the coronation records

tuples.episode_object: Otto the Third, the young emperor who wanted to rule from Rome and died at twenty-one
tuples.time_place_scope: Germany, Italy, and Rome at the turn of the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the attempt to make an imperial capital of a city whose citizens did not want one
tuples.evidence_lens: his diplomas, a Roman revolt's chronicle account, and manuscript illumination

tuples.episode_object: Henry the Third, the emperor who deposed three popes in a single synod
tuples.time_place_scope: Germany and central Italy in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the imperial right to appoint bishops and popes, and the reform movement it provoked
tuples.evidence_lens: synod records and reform correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Henry the Fourth, the emperor who stood in the snow at a mountain castle
tuples.time_place_scope: Germany, Saxony, and the Apennines in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the excommunication that releases vassals from their oaths, making penance a strategic move
tuples.evidence_lens: the letters of the dispute, and two competing narrative traditions

tuples.episode_object: Frederick the First, the emperor who fought Italian cities for thirty years over their taxes

tuples.mechanism: the renunciation of succession rights as a condition of returning home from exile
tuples.evidence_lens: the renunciation document and the property settlement negotiations

tuples.episode_object: Prince Henry, the emperor's brother who commanded a fleet and drove early motor cars
tuples.time_place_scope: Kiel and the Baltic in the twentieth century
tuples.mechanism: the royal officer in a technical service, where competence and rank are constantly negotiated
tuples.evidence_lens: the admiralty service records and the naval correspondence

tuples.episode_object: Louise Henriette of Orange, the electress whose marriage tied a German state to a republic
tuples.time_place_scope: Brandenburg and the Low Countries in the seventeenth century
tuples.mechanism: the dynastic marriage into a republic's ruling house, which imports its wars as well as its money
tuples.evidence_lens: the marriage contract and the subsidy treaties that followed

tuples.episode_object: Wilhelmine of Bayreuth, the sister whose memoirs described a brutal royal childhood
tuples.time_place_scope: Berlin and Bayreuth in the eighteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the royal memoir as the only surviving account of a court's private violence
tuples.evidence_lens: her own memoirs read against the official court and cabinet records

tuples.episode_object: Albrecht Achilles, the early margrave who wrote a law fixing the family's inheritance
tuples.time_place_scope: Brandenburg and Franconia in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the family statute making the mark indivisible, which prevented a century of partitions
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving family statute and the later succession records

tuples.episode_object: Sophia Charlotte, the queen whose court hosted philosophers and founded an academy
tuples.time_place_scope: Berlin and Hanover at the turn of the eighteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the court academy, endowed as a prestige institution and staffed by correspondence
tuples.evidence_lens: the academy's founding charter and her correspondence with its first members

tuples.episode_object: Elisabeth Ludovika of Bavaria, the queen whose confession complicated a Protestant court
tuples.time_place_scope: Berlin and Munich in the nineteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the confessionally mixed royal marriage, and the church settlements it forced
tuples.evidence_lens: the marriage negotiations and the concordat correspondence

tuples.episode_object: The First Emperor of Qin, the king who unified a country and standardised its axles
tuples.time_place_scope: the Wei valley and the whole conquered plain in the third century before our era
tuples.mechanism: standardisation of script, weights, currency, and cart axles as the machinery of unification
tuples.evidence_lens: excavated legal bamboo strips, a terracotta army, and standardised measure vessels

tuples.episode_object: The Second Emperor of Qin, the son whose accession may have rested on a forged letter
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the eastern provinces in the third century before our era
tuples.mechanism: the forged testament, and how quickly a new regime unravels when the succession is doubted
tuples.evidence_lens: a later grand history's account and excavated administrative documents

tuples.episode_object: Liu Bang, the village official who ended as founding emperor of a long dynasty
tuples.time_place_scope: the central plain and the Wei valley in the second century before our era
tuples.mechanism: the rebellion led by a commoner, and the noble followers who must then be pensioned or purged
tuples.evidence_lens: the founding annals, enfeoffment records, and early legal statutes

tuples.episode_object: Empress Lu, the widow who ruled through two child emperors and destroyed a rival family
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the second century before our era
tuples.mechanism: the empress dowager's regency and the promotion of her own clan to counterweight the imperial one
tuples.evidence_lens: the dynastic history's annals, which uniquely give her her own chapter

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Wen, the frugal ruler who cut taxes and mutilating punishments
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the provinces in the second century before our era
tuples.mechanism: the light-government approach, reducing corvee and tax to rebuild an exhausted population
tuples.evidence_lens: the recorded edicts abolishing punishments and the granary records

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Jing, the ruler who reduced the princes' territories and got a seven-kingdom revolt
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern kingdoms in the second century before our era
tuples.mechanism: the reduction of semi-independent princedoms, which provokes exactly the war it means to prevent
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals of the revolt and the subsequent administrative reorganisation

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Wu, the ruler who expanded to four frontiers and monopolised salt and iron
tuples.time_place_scope: the steppe, the western corridor, Korea, and the south in the second and first centuries
tuples.mechanism: the state monopoly on salt and iron, created to pay for frontier war and debated ever after
tuples.evidence_lens: a court debate transcript on the monopolies and frontier garrison documents

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Xuan, the great-grandson raised in a prison and brought to the throne
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the western frontier in the first century before our era
tuples.mechanism: the accession of a claimant with no court faction, chosen precisely because he had none
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals and the administrative documents of a well-recorded reign

tuples.episode_object: Wang Mang, the regent who took the throne outright and lost it to a flood
tuples.time_place_scope: the central plain and the Yellow River in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the reforming usurper whose land and currency changes collide with a river changing course
tuples.evidence_lens: the hostile dynastic history and the hydrological record of the river's shift

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Guangwu, the distant relative who restored a dynasty from the provinces
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern plain and a new capital in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the restoration built on great landowning families, whose power the new regime cannot reduce
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals, the household registration figures, and estate archaeology

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Ming, the ruler under whom a foreign religion is first officially noticed
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the western routes in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the arrival of a foreign religion through trade routes, and the court's cautious first sponsorship
tuples.evidence_lens: the traditional account of a dream and embassy, read against later temple records

tuples.episode_object: Empress Deng, the dowager who governed through famine, flood, and four emperors
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the provinces in the first and second centuries
tuples.mechanism: the dowager regency as an institution, staffed by palace eunuchs and her own kin
tuples.evidence_lens: the dynastic history's account and the relief edicts issued in her regency

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Huan, the ruler who used eunuchs to destroy a consort clan and could not control them after
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the alliance of an emperor with palace servants against his in-laws, and the faction it creates
tuples.evidence_lens: the histories of the proscriptions and the memorials of the scholar-officials

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Ling, the ruler who sold offices from a private treasury
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the provinces in the second century
tuples.mechanism: the sale of offices for a ruler's private purse, which converts administration into a market
tuples.evidence_lens: the recorded price lists and the memorials protesting them

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Xian, the last of the line, a hostage to three warlords in succession
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital, the Wei valley, and the eastern plain at the turn of the third century
tuples.mechanism: the puppet emperor whose person legitimises whichever general holds him
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals, the abdication edict, and the rival states' founding documents

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Zhang, the ruler who convened a conference to fix the meaning of the classics
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the state council on textual orthodoxy, which makes scholarship a branch of administration
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving record of the conference's conclusions

tuples.episode_object: Huo Guang, the regent who deposed an emperor after twenty-seven days
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the first century before our era
tuples.mechanism: the regent's power to depose, exercised once and remembered as a precedent for centuries
tuples.evidence_lens: the deposition memorial preserved in the dynastic history

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Ai, the young ruler whose favourite nearly received an abdication
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the first century before our era
tuples.mechanism: the court favourite raised to the highest office, and the officials who block a succession
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals and the memorials of the officials involved

tuples.episode_object: Empress Zhao Feiyan, the dancer who became empress and was blamed for a dynasty's decline
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the first century before our era
tuples.mechanism: the moral historiography that assigns a dynasty's fiscal failure to a consort's character
tuples.evidence_lens: the dynastic history's account read against the tax and granary record

tuples.episode_object: Gongsun Shu, the governor who declared his own empire in the west
tuples.time_place_scope: the western basin in the first century
tuples.mechanism: the provincial secession behind mountain passes, viable until the passes are forced
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals of the campaigns and the regional coinage

tuples.episode_object: Gaozu, the frontier commander who took a capital and let his sons fight for the rest
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern frontier and the Wei valley in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the founder who delegates the conquest to his sons and creates a succession contest
tuples.evidence_lens: the dynastic annals and the early administrative statutes

tuples.episode_object: Taizong, the second son who killed his brothers at a palace gate and reigned brilliantly
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital, the steppe, and the western corridor in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the fratricidal accession that later historiography excuses by pointing to the reign that followed
tuples.evidence_lens: the court policy dialogues compiled after his reign, and the annals' own awkwardness

tuples.episode_object: Gaozong, the emperor whose illness handed the government to his consort
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the Korean peninsula in the seventh century
tuples.mechanism: the transfer of administrative decision-making to a consort during a ruler's chronic illness
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals, the edicts issued jointly, and the campaign records

tuples.episode_object: Wu Zetian, the only woman to reign in her own name and under her own dynasty
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and a second eastern capital in the seventh and eighth centuries
tuples.mechanism: the founding of a new dynastic name by a consort, and the examinations used to build a new elite
tuples.evidence_lens: the examination records, the stele programme, and two hostile later histories

tuples.episode_object: Zhongzong, the emperor deposed by his mother and restored twenty years later
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and a provincial exile in the seventh and eighth centuries
tuples.mechanism: the emperor removed and restored by the same court, and the wife who repeats the pattern
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals and the records of the palace coups

tuples.episode_object: Ruizong, the brother who reigned twice and abdicated twice
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the seventh and eighth centuries
tuples.mechanism: the abdication used as a survival strategy in a court dominated by others
tuples.evidence_lens: the abdication edicts and the annals' chronology

tuples.episode_object: Xuanzong, the emperor whose long brilliant reign ended in a flight over mountains
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital, the north-eastern frontier, and the western basin in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the frontier military governorship, which concentrated troops and revenue far from the court
tuples.evidence_lens: the military commission records, the rebellion's chronicles, and census collapse figures

tuples.episode_object: Yang Guifei, the consort blamed for a rebellion she did not command
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and a mountain road in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the scapegoating of a consort at a mutiny, and the poetry that fixes the story afterwards
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals of the mutiny and the long narrative poem written a generation later

tuples.episode_object: Suzong, the heir who declared himself emperor in the north while his father fled south
tuples.time_place_scope: the north-western provinces in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the self-proclamation by an heir during a rebellion, ratified retroactively by the father
tuples.evidence_lens: the competing edicts of the same months and the campaign records

tuples.episode_object: Daizong, the emperor who bought peace with steppe cavalry and paid for it in silk
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the northern frontier in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the payment of allied cavalry in silk, which turns a textile tax into a defence budget
tuples.evidence_lens: the treaty records and the silk tribute accounts

tuples.episode_object: Dezong, the emperor whose new tax system replaced labour dues with two cash payments
tuples.time_place_scope: the empire in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the twice-yearly tax assessed on land and property rather than on individuals
tuples.evidence_lens: the reform edict and the subsequent revenue registers

tuples.episode_object: Xianzong, the emperor who brought the provinces back under the centre and was killed by eunuchs
tuples.time_place_scope: the eastern and central provinces in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the recovery of provincial obedience by war, and the palace army that grows to do it
tuples.evidence_lens: the campaign records and the palace army's establishment documents

tuples.episode_object: Wuzong, the emperor who dissolved thousands of monasteries and melted their bronze
tuples.time_place_scope: the empire in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the suppression of a religion for its untaxed land, labour, and metal
tuples.evidence_lens: the suppression edicts, a foreign monk's travel diary, and the coinage record

tuples.episode_object: The later Emperor Xuanzong, the ninth-century ruler who studied the classics and restored the archives
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the archival restoration after a suppression, and the limits of a paper recovery
tuples.evidence_lens: the reissued statutes and the library catalogues

tuples.episode_object: Empress Wei, the consort who tried to repeat a predecessor's path and failed
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the attempted repetition of a female accession without the institutional base the first one built
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals of the coup and the edicts issued in her brief ascendancy

tuples.episode_object: Princess Taiping, the daughter who made and unmade emperors and lost the last round
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the imperial princess as a faction leader with her own household and revenue
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals and the records of the estates confiscated after her fall

tuples.episode_object: Zhaozong, the emperor moved between warlords until one of them ended the dynasty

tuples.mechanism: the forced relocation of a capital, which destroys a court's archives and its independence
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals of the move and the archaeology of the abandoned capital

tuples.episode_object: Li Linfu, the chancellor who kept office for nineteen years
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the eighth century
tuples.mechanism: the long-serving chancellor who blocks rivals by promoting frontier generals of foreign origin
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals, the appointment records, and the later blame allocation

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Muzong, the young ruler who dissolved an army he had just used
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the northern provinces in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the demobilisation that saves money and immediately loses the provinces it had recovered
tuples.evidence_lens: the demobilisation edicts and the provincial revolt records

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Jingzong, the teenage ruler killed by his own polo attendants
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the ninth century
tuples.mechanism: the palace household as a lethal environment when discipline and favour are the same thing
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals' account of the killing and the succession that followed

tuples.episode_object: Taizu, the general handed a yellow robe by his own troops
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern plain in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the mutiny-accession staged by an army, and the founder's later disarming of his own generals
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals, the famous banquet account, and the early military reorganisation

tuples.episode_object: Taizong, the brother who succeeded instead of a son and never explained it well
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern plain and the northern frontier in the tenth century
tuples.mechanism: the fraternal succession that requires a story, and the story that keeps changing
tuples.evidence_lens: the competing accounts of the night of the succession in later compilations

tuples.episode_object: Zhenzong, the emperor who signed a treaty and paid an annual sum for a century of peace
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern frontier in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the annual payment treaty, cheaper than war and corrosive to a court's self-image
tuples.evidence_lens: the treaty text and the subsequent fiscal accounts

tuples.episode_object: Renzong, the emperor who let his officials argue policy in front of him for forty years
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the north-western frontier in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the remonstrance system, in which officials are paid to criticise and occasionally listened to
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving memorials and the reform debates of the period

tuples.episode_object: Shenzong, the emperor who backed a chancellor's reform programme against the whole bureaucracy
tuples.time_place_scope: the empire in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the state credit and procurement reforms, and the factional war they produced
tuples.evidence_lens: the reform statutes and the memorials of both factions

tuples.episode_object: Zhezong, the young emperor whose grandmother reversed the reforms and whose majority restored them
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the policy whiplash of a regency and a majority pulling in opposite directions
tuples.evidence_lens: the successive edicts repealing and reinstating the same measures

tuples.episode_object: Huizong, the emperor who painted birds while a northern army crossed the river
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the northern frontier at the turn of the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the alliance with a new steppe power against an old one, which replaces a manageable neighbour with an unmanageable one
tuples.evidence_lens: his surviving paintings and catalogues, and the campaign records

tuples.episode_object: Qinzong, the emperor who inherited a siege and was carried north as a prisoner
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital and the northern steppe in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the capture of an entire court, which forces a dynasty to restart from a surviving prince
tuples.evidence_lens: the siege accounts, the ransom negotiations, and the captivity records

tuples.episode_object: Gaozong, the surviving prince who rebuilt a dynasty in the south and killed his best general
tuples.time_place_scope: the lower river valleys and a southern capital in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the peace faction's victory over a war faction, secured by executing the war party's commander
tuples.evidence_lens: the peace treaty terms and the trial record of the general

tuples.episode_object: Empress Dowager Liu, the regent who wore imperial robes but stopped short of the title
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the regency that adopts imperial ceremonial without claiming the throne
tuples.evidence_lens: the court ritual records and the annals' careful wording

tuples.episode_object: Xiaozong, the adopted heir who tried to reopen a war and settled for good government
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern capital and the river frontier in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the adoption of a collateral heir when a direct line fails, and the legitimacy work it requires
tuples.evidence_lens: the adoption edicts and the campaign and treaty records

tuples.episode_object: Ningzong, the emperor under whom a chancellor started and lost a northern war
tuples.time_place_scope: the river frontier in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the war launched by a minister to secure his own position, and the head sent north to end it
tuples.evidence_lens: the campaign records and the peace terms

tuples.episode_object: Lizong, the emperor who allied with a steppe power against a northern neighbour a second time
tuples.time_place_scope: the river frontier and the northern plain in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the repetition of a fatal alliance strategy by a court that had recorded its first failure
tuples.evidence_lens: the diplomatic records and the campaign chronicles

tuples.episode_object: Duzong, the emperor whose reign is measured by the length of a single siege
tuples.time_place_scope: the middle river fortresses in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the fortress siege lasting years, which absorbs a dynasty's whole military capacity
tuples.evidence_lens: the siege accounts from both sides and the fortress archaeology

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Bing, the child carried into the sea by an official at the end
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern coast in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the flight of a court by sea, and the end of a dynasty at a coastal battle
tuples.evidence_lens: the chronicles of the final campaign and the commemorative sites

tuples.episode_object: Wang Anshi, the reform chancellor whose whole programme rested on one emperor's support
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the reformer whose programme depends entirely on one ruler's continuing support
tuples.evidence_lens: the memorials, the reform statutes, and the record of his dismissals and recalls

tuples.episode_object: Empress Yang, the consort who helped arrange a chancellor's death
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern capital in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the inner palace as a decision point in the removal of a chief minister
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals and the memorials surrounding the minister's fall

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Yingzong, the adopted heir whose accession caused a three-year argument about titles
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the eleventh century
tuples.mechanism: the ritual dispute over what to call an adopted emperor's natural father
tuples.evidence_lens: the surviving memorials of the ritual controversy

tuples.episode_object: Yue Fei, the commander executed on a charge nobody could specify
tuples.time_place_scope: the river frontier and the southern capital in the twelfth century
tuples.mechanism: the political trial of a popular commander, and the posthumous rehabilitation that follows
tuples.evidence_lens: the trial record, the rehabilitation edict, and the later shrine cult

tuples.episode_object: Emperor Duanzong, the boy proclaimed on a boat off the southern coast
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern islands in the thirteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the court in flight, issuing edicts from ships with no territory to administer
tuples.evidence_lens: the chronicles of the flight and the surviving edict texts

tuples.episode_object: The Hongwu Emperor, the orphaned monk who founded a dynasty and abolished his own chancellery
tuples.time_place_scope: the lower river valleys and a southern capital in the fourteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the abolition of the chancellor's office, which concentrated every decision on one desk
tuples.evidence_lens: his own instructions to descendants, the purge records, and the land registers

tuples.episode_object: The Jianwen Emperor, the grandson who tried to reduce his uncles and lost a palace fire
tuples.time_place_scope: the southern capital in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the reduction of princely appanages, which provoked the strongest prince into rebellion
tuples.evidence_lens: the campaign records and the later suppression of his reign era in official documents

tuples.episode_object: The Yongle Emperor, the uncle who took a throne, moved a capital, and sent out treasure fleets
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern frontier, a new capital, and the Indian Ocean in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the ocean-going tribute fleet as a diplomatic instrument, and the cost that ended it
tuples.evidence_lens: the voyage steles, the shipyard records, and the encyclopaedia compiled in his reign

tuples.episode_object: The Zhengtong Emperor, the ruler captured on campaign and later restored
tuples.time_place_scope: the northern steppe frontier and the capital in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the captured emperor whose court simply enthrones his brother and refuses the ransom
tuples.evidence_lens: the campaign account of the defeat and the succession edicts

tuples.episode_object: The Jingtai Emperor, the brother who held the throne and lost it when the captive came home
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the restoration coup, in which a returned predecessor is smuggled back onto his own throne
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals and the posthumous demotion records

tuples.episode_object: The Chenghua Emperor, the ruler dominated by a much older consort
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the palace favourite who controls access, and the secret birth of an heir kept from her
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals and the palace administration records

tuples.episode_object: The Hongzhi Emperor, the ruler who had one wife and no concubines
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the fifteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the monogamous emperor, and the succession risk a court accepts in exchange for a quiet palace
tuples.evidence_lens: the annals, the ritual records, and the official histories' unusual praise

tuples.episode_object: The Zhengde Emperor, the ruler who gave himself a military title and a second name

tuples.mechanism: the emperor who appoints himself a general to escape the constraints of his own office
tuples.evidence_lens: the memorials protesting the tours and the edicts issued under his invented title

tuples.episode_object: The Jiajing Emperor, the cousin who fought a twenty-year argument about whom to call father
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the sixteenth century
tuples.mechanism: the great ritual controversy, in which a succession from a collateral line is fought out as liturgy
tuples.evidence_lens: the memorials of the controversy and the punishments recorded against officials

tuples.episode_object: The Wanli Emperor, the ruler who stopped attending court for decades

tuples.mechanism: the strike by a monarch against his own bureaucracy, leaving offices unfilled for years
tuples.evidence_lens: the memorials complaining of vacancies and the campaign finance records

tuples.episode_object: The Taichang Emperor, the ruler who reigned twenty-nine days and died after taking red pills
tuples.time_place_scope: the capital in the seventeenth century
tuples.mechanism: the medical scandal at a succession, which becomes a factional weapon for a generation
tuples.evidence_lens: the case records of the three palace mysteries and the subsequent memorials

tuples.episode_object: The Tianqi Emperor, the carpenter emperor whose eunuch ran the state

tuples.mechanism: the eunuch secretariat that reads and answers memorials on a disengaged ruler's behalf
tuples.evidence_lens: the memorials, the proscription lists of the opposing faction, and shrine records

tuples.episode_object: The Chongzhen Emperor, the last of the line, who hanged himself on a hill behind his palace
